problem:
The intake module `.ok-planner/bin/issues` (ok suite v25.0.0) refuses every verb but `import` while a markdown file stands directly under `.ok-planner/issues/`. `read_store` lists that folder before each verb and raises:

So a project upgraded to v25 cannot file one issue until the owner converts every leftover markdown file. Every writer of the intake stops: `/converge`'s owner list, `/triage-issues`, the audit's judge, `/plan-sprint`, and a human filer. The intake then took no new issue until the owner committed a fix by hand.

problem:
The suite used to ship a separate workspaces family. Its estate, `.ok-workspaces/`, held a script that mints a tag for a verification run: `run-tag`, or in older projects `src-tag`. The suite has since folded that family into ok-planner, whose own copy is `.ok-planner/bin/run-tag`. When `/ok` migrates a project, the converge core keeps the old copy, because project files still call it. The core then offers only to delete it, and recommends declining while any file names it. It offers no way to move those callers to the suite's copy. An owner who follows the recommendation keeps the retired script, and with it the retired estate directory, forever.

The same core handles the same job differently for the retired lint: it drafts each caller's repoint as an offer. The owner's direction is that neither case asks: the script is suite-owned, so the suite may relocate it and update its callers. The current design does not allow that, because the callers are project files.

## Mechanism

[retired_script_offer](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L1498) builds one `retired-script` offer per kept script. Its only fix is `delete <path>`. It finds callers with [script_callers](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L1492), a `git grep -F` on the literal path, and recommends `decline` while that grep returns any file. [The administration document's kept-scripts step](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md#L218) says the same. While the old copy stays, the workspaces migration keeps the `.ok-workspaces/` directory that holds it.

The lint's retirement uses a `script-path` offer. [script_path_offers](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L1649) finds each tracked project file that names the lint or `catalog-toc` under `.ok-plumbline/bin/` and drafts the whole new file with each listed line repointed to `.ok-planner/bin/`. `resolve` refuses a draft that changes any other line. The list of paths it repoints, [RETIRED_SCRIPT_PATHS](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L1633), names only those two. No run-tag counterpart exists.

The core already rewrites some stale suite paths in owner files with no offer. [The administration document's exceptions](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md#L332) list the review loop's `config.json` entries, the lint config's two citation templates, and a live sprint's boilerplate lines. A project's source files are not among them.

The kept scripts are not all drop-ins for the suite's copy. The old `run-tag` printed a fresh random `run-<12 hex>` on each call, as [the suite's copy](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/run-tag) does. The old `src-tag` printed `src-` and the first 12 hex of the working tree's git tree hash, so the same tree gave the same tag on every call. A caller that calls `src-tag` twice in one run, once to build and once to verify, gets one tag. After a repoint to `run-tag` it gets two. The old `port-block` computes ports from a job name, and the suite's `port-block` reads them back by run tag, so its callers have no drop-in at all.

The owner met this in the consumer project linescout, migrated from v23.0.0 to v24.0.0. Five tracked files called the old copy, `.ok-workspaces/bin/src-tag`. The offer listed four of them. The fifth, `src/gridiq/cli/instance.py`, builds the path from parts, so the literal grep missed it, as the offer's own text warns. The owner repointed all five by hand.

## State of play

The old copy keeps working, so nothing breaks today. No accept-list entry covers the gap as a defect. The old `run-tag` copy also lacks the suite's check for an empty random read, which matters only when the OS fails a random read. [decision:whole-file-ownership](.ok-planner/design/decisions/whole-file-ownership.md) says the core "never edits a file a human also edits", and that anything else at a path the suite cares about "is presented for the owner's decision". It migrates mechanically only "the suite's own retired-layout content". A repoint with no offer therefore needs the decision to class a line that names a retired suite script's path as that content. The plumbline cheatsheet's Uniformity rule ("One idiom per job") asks that the lint and run-tag repoints take one shape. No repoint can find a path built in code.

## Options

The ruling decides how converge moves the callers of a retired suite script to the suite's copy, and whether it asks first.

Then have the core repoint every such line for the lint, `catalog-toc`, and the old `run-tag` and `src-tag` copies, name each rewritten file in its report, retire the `script-path` offer, and remove the old copy and its estate once no tracked file names it. The report line for each repointed `src-tag` caller says the tag is now fresh on every call. The old `port-block` keeps its `retired-script` offer.

messages.text: The converge should not enumerate artifacts to look for. Revised to your direction. The options now choose how converge finds stale content, not which of four items it fixes, since the fixed list is why all four passed. Three facts bound the new shape.

First, a general audit replaces a stated rule. [The administration document](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md#L3) says the front door reads it and "nothing here is improvised", and [concept:true-up](.ok-planner/design/concepts/true-up.md) says converge migrates "every retired layout it recognizes". Both need amending, and the recommendation names both.

Second, a project from any earlier version is already found. [decision:filesystem-discovery-markers](.ok-planner/design/decisions/filesystem-discovery-markers.md) has the front door honor every documented pre-migration marker. What is missing is the migration of content no release named, which is what the audit adds.

Third, [decision:whole-file-ownership](.ok-planner/design/decisions/whole-file-ownership.md) still sets consent. The suite's own retired-layout content migrates without asking. Owner-declared configuration, such as a new `folders` key, is written only from the owner's explicit answer, and the root `CLAUDE.md` is untouchable. I read "preserving and updating any user configurations that are still supported" as working within those rules, so the audit drafts owner configuration as offers. If you mean it to update owner configuration without asking, the recommendation's flip case covers that: it amends the same decision as the sibling run-tag issue, and the two are best ruled together.

Option A

options.label: A
options.text: **A migration audit after the core's moves.** After the core moves every retired layout it recognizes, the front door's administration runs an audit over the estate and every tracked project file the suite reads or governs: `.ok-planner/config.json`, the review loop's `config.json`, the hook wiring in `.claude/settings.json`, the project's own rules files, and the root `CLAUDE.md`. The audit reads them against the carried version's documentation of what each setting and path means. It finds each value, path, or reference the current version no longer supports, and each setting the current version newly needs, such as `folders` for a project whose sprints name outside paths. It sorts each finding by [decision:whole-file-ownership](.ok-planner/design/decisions/whole-file-ownership.md): suite retired-layout content the core rewrites with no offer, owner configuration drafted as an offer, and the root `CLAUDE.md` as a report line. Diagnose reports agreement only once the audit finds nothing pending. Cost: an agent's judgment enters a step that today improvises nothing, so two runs over one project may find different things; the audit is only as complete as the documentation it reads against; and each `/ok` spends one agent's reading of the project.

options.label: B
options.text: **A mechanical check against a declared schema.** The carried version declares every configuration key it reads and every path it ever retired. The core flags each value outside that schema and each retired path in any tracked file, and offers or rewrites each by the ownership rule. Cost: a schema per configuration file, kept in step with every tool that reads it; and no schema can judge prose or infer a value such as `folders`.

options.label: C
options.text: **A wider fixed list.** The core adds the four items: retired estates out of `ignore` and `exclude` with no offer, a `folders` offer drafted from the sprints' outside paths, `review-wording` over project-owned rules files, and a report line for the root `CLAUDE.md`. Cost: each release must name each stale entry, and the next one the list misses passes silently, as linescout's four did.

options.label: D
options.text: **Keep as is.** Cost: every migrated project carries whatever the list misses, and a multi-folder project repeats linescout's failures until its owner reads the release notes.

problem:
When `/ok` moves a project from v23 to v24, the converge core moves the retired estates (`.ok-plumbline/`, `.ok-workspaces/`, `.ok-review/`) into `.ok-planner/`. It then prints cleanup offers for the stale entries it knows about. Once the owner settles those offers, diagnose prints "in agreement with carried v24.0.0". In the consumer project linescout, four stale items survived that message, and no offer named any of them:

1. **No `folders` key.** linescout owns two folders beside its root, `../image` and `../runtime`. Its sprints already list them under `## Paths outside the project root`. v24 adds a `folders` list to `.ok-planner/config.json`. The lint, its edit hook, the review loop, the audit's sweep, and the surface extractor all read that list. The migration never proposed it. Until the owner added the key by hand, the lint failed every design citation under `../runtime`, and a converge fixer deleted a citation block to make its check pass.
2. **`ignore` names a retired estate.** `.ok-planner/config.json` kept `".ok-plumbline/"` in `ignore`. The migration moved the old lint config byte for byte and rewrites nothing in its `ignore` list.
3. **The review loop's `exclude` names retired estates.** `.ok-planner/review/config.json` kept `".ok-plumbline/"` and `".ok-workspaces/"` in `exclude`. [The `.ok-review/` migration](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md#L291) already rewrites, with no offer, the `.ok-review/` entry of that list, and the plumbline migration rewrites every `standards` and `checks` entry that names a moved path. Neither touches the other two retired estates. The only `exclude` offer covers `.claude/` and `.ok-planner/`.
4. **Project prose names a retired family's rules.** The project's own rule `.claude/rules/dev-loop.md` said verification runs the per-run image "the ok-workspaces rules require". The core removes the ok-workspaces rules file, and that rule now lives in the ok-planner cheatsheet. [The `review-wording` offer](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md#L94) catches a retired estate path in `review/project.md` alone. No offer reads the project's own rules files or its root `CLAUDE.md`.

The four items share one cause: the migration is a list. The core moves owner configuration as it stands and fixes only the entries a release named. [The administration document](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md#L3) says the front door reads it and "nothing here is improvised", and [concept:true-up](.ok-planner/design/concepts/true-up.md) says converge migrates "every retired layout it recognizes from an earlier release". Every entry outside that list passes silently, and diagnose reports agreement because no offer is pending. A project that skips releases meets more such entries, since each release's list names only what that release retired. Items 2 and 3 name directories that no longer exist, so they change nothing a tool does today. They are dead configuration that the next reader must puzzle out. Item 1 cost real work: a lint failing on code the project owns, and a fixer that deleted citations to quiet it. Item 4 is guidance an agent reads that points at a file that is gone.

[story:converge-project-estate](.ok-planner/design/stories/converge-project-estate.md) asks that the owner can bring the whole suite presence, "including what an earlier release laid out", current "in one deliberate act, so that upgrading the suite never costs me work I wrote". [story:project-spans-folders](.ok-planner/design/stories/project-spans-folders.md) asks "that no check the suite runs over my project misses code I own". [decision:filesystem-discovery-markers](.ok-planner/design/decisions/filesystem-discovery-markers.md) already finds a project from any earlier release by its documented pre-migration markers. [decision:whole-file-ownership](.ok-planner/design/decisions/whole-file-ownership.md) sets the consent rules. The suite's own retired-layout content is migrated mechanically. Owner-declared configuration is written only as transcription of the owner's explicit answers. The consumer's own rules file and memory file are categorically untouchable. [decision:project-declares-its-folders](.ok-planner/design/decisions/project-declares-its-folders.md) keeps one `folders` list, defaulting to the root alone, and says a sprint's outside folders stay an addition for that sprint's change.

No accept-list entry covers these items as defects. The administration document does not promise that "in agreement" means every configuration value is current. The owner filed this as a change to the converge core: "it should merge/fix all relevant configurations". The owner has since directed that converge not enumerate what to look for, but audit the estates and the project in general and migrate the whole project from whatever earlier version it comes from, preserving and updating each owner configuration the current version still supports. The sibling issue `retired-run-tag-callers-never-repointed` comes from the same migration and the same report.

## Options

The ruling decides how converge finds what an earlier release left stale: a fixed list, a mechanical check against what the current version declares, or a general audit.

recommendation.text:
Option A. Amend [concept:true-up](.ok-planner/design/concepts/true-up.md) to say that converge migrates the whole project from any earlier release: the core moves every retired layout it recognizes, and then an audit of the estate and the project finds every remaining value, path, or reference the current version no longer supports, and every setting it newly needs, and brings each current. Amend the administration document to define that audit step, what it reads, and its report, in place of its claim that nothing in it is improvised. The audit sorts each finding by [decision:whole-file-ownership](.ok-planner/design/decisions/whole-file-ownership.md). The suite's retired-layout content, such as a retired estate named in `ignore` or `exclude`, the core rewrites with no offer. Owner-declared configuration, such as a `folders` list drafted from the sprints' outside paths, goes to the owner as an offer with a draft. The root `CLAUDE.md` gets a report line naming its stale lines. Diagnose reports agreement only once the audit finds nothing pending.

Rationale: the owner directed a general audit over a list of artifacts to look for. [story:converge-project-estate](.ok-planner/design/stories/converge-project-estate.md) promises "one deliberate act" that brings "what an earlier release laid out" current, and a fixed list keeps that promise only for what each release remembered to name; linescout's four items show the gap. [story:project-spans-folders](.ok-planner/design/stories/project-spans-folders.md) makes a missing `folders` list the costliest miss, and only a reader that knows what the key is for can propose it, which rules out option B. [decision:filesystem-discovery-markers](.ok-planner/design/decisions/filesystem-discovery-markers.md) already finds a project from any earlier release, so the audit adds no discovery of its own. [decision:whole-file-ownership](.ok-planner/design/decisions/whole-file-ownership.md)'s consent rules stay as written, so the audit changes what converge finds, not what it may write unasked. The flip case: if the owner means the audit to update owner configuration without asking, that is an amendment to [decision:whole-file-ownership](.ok-planner/design/decisions/whole-file-ownership.md) as well, best ruled with retired-run-tag-callers-never-repointed, which widens the same decision.

ruling.text: Option A

title: The v24 migration calls a project "in agreement" while its configuration still names retired estates and lacks the folders it owns

messages.text: "The run still has to undo its own edit to such a file when a fix fails" why are these files edited at all if they are not allowed to be "fixed"? Why wouldn't any file updated during a sprint execution be fixable? "When a fix fails" how can a fix "fail"? If the fix must have a judgment, then we'd expect an issue to be filed. Otherwise, we're unclear how a fix can "fail".

No agent of the run may edit those files. The fix prompt says "Edit no file the fix line rule above leaves alone", and a fixer whose defect can only be fixed there declines it and records it for the owner list ([fix.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/fix.md#L59)). An edit happens only when a fixer breaks that rule. Nothing stops the write, so the bytes land in the tree, and the verifier sends any change that edited such a file back ([verify.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/verify.md#L28)). The backout's exception exists to clean up that breach. It allows no fix.

Which files are fixable depends on who owns a file, not on who changed it last. [decision:runs-fix-what-the-project-owns](.ok-planner/design/decisions/runs-fix-what-the-project-owns.md) says so: "The line follows ownership, not location." A sprint's build applies its corpus deltas to `.ok-planner/design/`. Certification's fixers still leave those files alone, because the corpus changes only through a sprint's deltas. A defect whose fix lies there goes to the intake as a judgment issue. Every other file a sprint changed is fixable. Making the corpus files a sprint changed fixable during that sprint's certification would change the decision. Rule that on this issue or file it as its own issue, and `/plan-sprint` takes it up.

A fix fails when a verifier sends it back. The verifier reads only the fixer's change. problem:
A `/converge` run finds defects and sends fixer agents to fix them. [decision:runs-fix-what-the-project-owns](.ok-planner/design/decisions/runs-fix-what-the-project-owns.md) puts five kinds of file off limits to every agent of the run: the design corpus and coding standards, a suite-owned file, an owner's declaration, a record, and a document the release regenerates. No agent may edit one. A fixer can still edit one by mistake, because nothing stops the write. A verifier then sends that fix back. When a defect's fixes are sent back up to the run's limit, the defect is stuck. A backout agent then restores every file its fixes changed, including a left-alone one. The backout prompt allows that restore. The skill's own list of exceptions does not mention it. So two texts of the same skill disagree about who may touch a left-alone file.

## How a fix fails

A fixer stages a change and marks its defect fixed. A verifier reads only that change. It sends the change back when the harm still stands, when the change adds a harm, or when the change edits a file the fix line rule leaves alone ([verify.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/verify.md#L28)). Each send-back raises the defect's count of send-backs. At `fix.max_kickbacks` the defect is stuck ([converge SKILL.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/SKILL.md#L109)). [decision:converge-finds-then-fixes](.ok-planner/design/decisions/converge-finds-then-fixes.md) treats such a defect as "no longer mechanical, because what fixes it is a judgment". The run backs the stuck defect's change out, so the tree keeps only changes a verifier accepted. The owner list files the defect as a judgment issue with each fix tried and each verifier's reason.

## Mechanism

Three texts carry the rule:

- The shared rule `{{FIX-LINE-RULE}}` in [coding-rules.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_converge/coding-rules.md#L60-L90) says the run "leaves five kinds of file alone, and no agent of the run edits one". Every merge, fix, verify, backout, sprint review, and sprint pass prompt pastes it.
- [converge SKILL.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/SKILL.md#L159), under "What stays outside this skill", says no agent edits a file of the five kinds, and that "the one exception is the owner-list agent, which writes the intake".
- [backout.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/backout.md#L32) pastes the shared rule, then tells the backout agent to back out each file the stuck defect's fixes changed "even where the fix line rule above leaves that file alone: the backout undoes the run's own edit and makes none of its own".

The fix prompt forbids the edit ([fix.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/fix.md#L59)), and no tool enforces it. A fixer's edit to a left-alone file reaches the tree before a verifier reads it. [review:cmd_backouts](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/review#L1195) files a backout over every file the stuck defect's fix tasks staged, whatever its kind, and the backout must restore that file. So the backout prompt states a real second exception. The skill's list names only the owner-list agent.

A fixer in run converge-2026-10-05T024119 wrote the exception into the backout prompt alone, because the shared rule lay outside its task's files, and recorded the choice as call i48.

## State of play

No harm has been observed. The backout agent reads its own exception. The risk lies with another reader. The orchestrator or a verifier could read SKILL.md's "the one exception" and treat a backout's restore as a breach. No accept-list entry covers the disagreement today.

The decision itself is not wrong. Restoring the owner's bytes undoes the run's edit and makes no new one, so the file ends as the run found it. The decision's rationale concerns changes a run makes ("the next converge overwrites a local edit"; "changing either is the owner's act"), not undoing them.

## Options

The ruling decides whether the backout's restore of a left-alone file needs a corpus commitment, or only an accurate list in the skill.

messages.text:
A divider is any comment of punctuation alone, whatever its length. Drop the length bound.

Rationale: The label exists to sort violations by the action the owner takes. The audit defines the mechanical cluster as violations whose fix is fully determined. A comment with no letter or digit says nothing, so its fix is always a delete, at any length. A length bound sends a contentless comment to the prose cluster, which asks the owner to read it for a constraint it cannot hold. The other two options keep a threshold that no project rule or corpus artifact explains. Flip case: if the owner finds short punctuation-only comments that carry meaning, such as an elision marker in a code example that the owner keeps on purpose, a bound keeps those out of the delete bucket. Then the stripped-text bound is the better threshold, because it stops counting the marker.

options.label: A
options.text: **Any punctuation-only comment is a divider, whatever its length.** Cost: `// --` and its kin move from `disallowed-prose` to `divider`, so the audit treats them as mechanical deletes. A bare `//` or `#` with no text also becomes a divider. It is deleted either way.

options.label: B
options.text: **Keep the eight-character bound on the source line.** Cost: an arbitrary threshold that counts the marker, so two dividers of one style label differently.

options.label: C
options.text: **Bound the punctuation after the marker is stripped.** Cost: a new threshold to pick, which must differ by marker style and still labels by length.

problem:
`plumbline patterns` groups the lint's comment violations by shape, so the audit can sort them by the action each needs. One shape is `divider`: a comment made of punctuation alone, such as `// ========`. The lint labels a comment `divider` only when its trimmed source line is at least eight characters long. A shorter punctuation-only comment, such as `// --`, falls through and gets the label `disallowed-prose`.

The label does not change the lint's verdict. Both labels are `comment-hygiene` violations, and the exit code is the same. The label matters to the audit. Its lint sweep puts dividers in the mechanical cluster, where the fix is fully determined: delete. Prose can carry a real constraint, so a reader of a `disallowed-prose` cluster must look at each member before acting. A short divider labelled prose therefore leaves the mechanical bucket and costs the owner a look it does not need.

The eight-character bound counts the comment marker with the rest of the line. `// --` is 5 characters, `// ----` is 7, and `//------` is 8. Two dividers of one style can thus label differently by a character or two. No concept, story, decision, or practice defines a divider. The term appears only in the lint and in the audit's sweep instructions.

The bound has a history. A fixer in run converge-2026-10-05T024119 rebuilt the shape check to fix defect i38. That fixer kept the base's bound on the source line, because no bound on the stripped comment text reproduces the base: stripped length varies by marker style (`// -----` gives 5, `/* ** */` gives 1). The fixer recorded the other reading, no bound at all, as an open call.

## Options

No stated rule decides between them. The ruling decides what the lint counts as a divider.

## Mechanism

[`plugins/ok-conduct/hooks/session-start`](plugins/ok-conduct/hooks/session-start) writes the line into every session. The only copy of the skill is [`plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/ok-version/SKILL.md`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/ok-version/SKILL.md), in the family the front door carries. The converge core copies it into a project's `.claude/skills/` only when the project integrates ok-planner. `plugins/ok/skills` holds only `ok`, and `plugins/ok-conduct` ships no skill. `/ok` accepts a declined bootstrap and records the project as "not integrated (declined)". `/ok` reports suite versions, but not the governing conduct. It also updates plugins before it reports, so it is no read-only check.

A driver in run converge-2026-10-05T024119 found this (failure i4). The merge agent confirmed it under [A9](.ok-planner/review/catalog/accept.md#L17): the hook tells the session something false that the user acts on. The hook line stood the same at the run's base, so the defect lay outside that run's scope. A sprint driver recorded the open question as call i24: "The corpus does not decide which."

## State of play

The corpus pulls two ways. [concept:conduct](.ok-planner/design/concepts/conduct.md) says the conduct governs "in every project and session the user runs", and lies "outside any project's vendored presence". [decision:vendored-skills](.ok-planner/design/decisions/vendored-skills.md) keeps the machine-shared layer to "the administrator, the conduct, and the web setup skills". The version skill belongs to the vendored layer. [story:see-governing-versions](.ok-planner/design/stories/see-governing-versions.md) does not say whether a user with only the conduct counts as "a suite consumer". Its goal is "so that version drift is visible and convergence stays my deliberate act", and convergence is the act of `/ok` in an integrated project. Between sessions, the governing conduct and the installed one load from the same copy, so they differ only after a plugin update mid-session. A new session ends that gap.

## Options

The ruling decides where the suite owes the version view, and so what the conduct's hook may point to.

recommendation.text:
Option C. Drop the clause "/ok-version reports the conduct actually governing" from the conduct's session-start hook, so its line states the installed conduct version and names no command. Amend [story:see-governing-versions](.ok-planner/design/stories/see-governing-versions.md) to read: "As the owner of a project that integrates ok-planner, I want to see which plugin version governs my current session beside the version this project's vendored layer carries, so that version drift is visible and convergence stays my deliberate act."

Rationale: the owner's comment drops the pointer from the conduct. [concept:conduct](.ok-planner/design/concepts/conduct.md) places the conduct outside any project's vendored presence, and a conduct line that points at a vendored skill crosses that boundary. Option B keeps the crossing and hard-codes ok-planner's layout into the personal layer. Option A widens the machine-shared layer that [decision:vendored-skills](.ok-planner/design/decisions/vendored-skills.md) keeps small on purpose, to serve a drift that a conduct-only user ends by starting a new session. Option D turns a read-only check into an administration act. Without the story amendment, the story would still owe the view to a conduct-only user. The story's own goal names convergence, which only an integrated project performs, so narrowing the actor states what it already means. The wording is the one its sibling installed-version-entry-selection recommends, so the two rulings amend the story once. The flip case: if the owner reads the hook's whole line as install information Claude Code's plugin manager already shows, the session-start hook goes entirely. Nothing reads its line.

messages.text: An agent is driving the converge. We don't understand what "a failed file move is". If the file is locked and can't be moved, or the classifier prevents the file from being moved, then converge can stop and ask the user to resolve the issue. In no event should converge be allowed to leave he project migration in an incomplete state.

The agent that drives `/ok` moves no file itself. On your consent it runs one command, `converge resolve markdown-intake:.ok-planner/issues --from <draft>`, and the converge core makes every write inside that command ([ok SKILL.md](plugins/ok/skills/ok/SKILL.md#L114)). The permission classifier approves or refuses that command as a whole. A refusal writes nothing, so the classifier cannot stop a migration partway. A failed move happens inside the core. [converge:move_path](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L585) runs one `git mv` per file, and git refuses it when another git process holds `.git/index.lock`, for example an editor's git integration or a commit in another terminal. A folder the file system will not write refuses the same way. The core has already imported the records when this happens, so it stops between the two stores.

I took your comment as the bar for the fix: converge never leaves the migration incomplete, and it stops and asks where a move cannot happen. The old recommendation, Resume, leaves a half-migrated state for the next `/ok` to finish, so it no longer fits. I rewrote the problem, the options, and the recommendation around that bar. The new recommendation checks every cause the core can see before its first write and refuses with the cause named. That refusal is the stop-and-ask you describe. It then moves every file before the import, in one `git mv` call that moves every file or none. Undoing an import would mean deleting records, which the intake format forbids, so the files move first.

problem: rewritten whole around the owner's comment. A new section, What a failed move is, says the core makes every move inside one consented command and names what makes `git mv` refuse. State of play records the owner's bar and three facts that bound a fix: two stores share no transaction, an import cannot be undone because records are never deleted, and one `git mv` call moves every tracked file or none. options: added A (check, move in one call, then import), which absorbs the old D (validate, then move in one call, then import). The old A, B, and C are now B, C, and D, and the costs of B and D name the owner's bar. recommendation: changed from Resume to option A, because the owner's comment rules out a resumable half state.
Option A

options.label: A
options.text: **Check, move in one call, then import.** Before its first write, the migration checks every cause of failure it can see: the index lock free, each folder writable, each destination free, and the whole import through a dry run of the intake module. A failed check refuses the migration with nothing written and names the cause for the owner to settle. The migration then moves every tracked file in one `git mv` call, which moves every file or none, and each untracked file by rename, then imports. Where the import still fails, it moves the files back and stops with the cause named, so the project ends as it began. Cost: the intake module needs a dry-run verb. The move back is a second write, run only on a failure the dry run did not foresee. A process killed between the move and the import still leaves the issues in history and out of the store.

options.label: B
options.text: **Resume.** Keep import first, then move. The next `/ok` recognizes a file whose record already stands, matched by the record's `source` field, and offers to move it without importing again. Cost: the half-migrated state stays reachable and becomes a documented state, which the owner's bar rules out.

options.label: C
options.text: **Move first, roll back on refusal.** Move every file, then import, and move the files back where the import refuses. This is the first fix tried. Cost: with no dry run the move back runs on every refused import, a second write that can itself fail, and a verifier already sent this fix back.

options.label: D
options.text: **Move first, import later.** Move every file, then import. Where the import refuses, leave the files in history, and have the next `/ok` import from there. Cost: between the two runs the issues stand in neither the live intake nor the store, which the owner's bar rules out.

problem:
The suite is retiring its old intake, one markdown file per issue, for one JSON Lines file of records ([decision:issue-records-in-one-file](.ok-planner/design/decisions/issue-records-in-one-file.md)). The front door's converge core migrates a project in one accepted offer. It imports a record for each issue file, then moves each file to the history folder. The same order serves the older `design/tensions/` layout. If one move fails partway, the project holds records in the new store while some source files still stand in the live folder. No complete run produces that state. The next `/ok` then offers the migration again and imports the unmoved issues a second time under new ids. That breaks [story:converge-project-estate](.ok-planner/design/stories/converge-project-estate.md), which promises an upgrade "in one deliberate act" that "never costs me work I wrote". Accept-list entries [A1](.ok-planner/review/catalog/accept.md#L9) (stored state half-changed) and [A7](.ok-planner/review/catalog/accept.md#L15) (accepted data doubled) name both harms.

## What a failed move is

The agent that drives `/ok` moves no file itself. On the owner's consent it runs one command, `converge resolve <offer> --from <draft>`, and the converge core makes every write inside it ([ok SKILL.md](plugins/ok/skills/ok/SKILL.md#L114)). The permission classifier approves or refuses that command as a whole, and a refusal writes nothing. A move fails inside the core when git or the file system refuses it. Git refuses a `git mv` while another git process holds `.git/index.lock`, for example an editor's git integration or a commit in another terminal. The file system refuses a folder it will not write. Either refusal raises in the middle of the core's loop.

## Mechanism

`resolve` in [admin/converge](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L2781-L2807) handles the `markdown-intake` and `tensions` offers. It writes two stores in sequence. First, [converge:import_issues](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L2069) writes every record to `.ok-planner/issues.jsonl` in one transaction of the intake module. Then a loop calls [converge:move_path](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L585) once per file. Each call runs its own `git mv`, or a plain rename for an untracked file. A failure raises mid-loop. Nothing rolls the import back, and nothing records which files moved.

The owner then meets two things. Every intake verb but `import` refuses while a markdown file stands under `.ok-planner/issues/`, and names the `markdown-intake` offer. So the owner runs `/ok` again. The offer gives each file its `issue:` value as its id only where no open issue already carries that id. The first run imported that id, so the offer derives a fresh one, `<slug>-2`. The draft checks compare the draft to the offer's ids and sources, never to records already in the store. The import skips a record only when the same id holds identical content. An owner who accepts imports each unmoved issue a second time.

## State of play

Each step checks its own inputs. The draft checks refuse a malformed draft. The intake module checks every record before it writes any and refuses the whole import, so a refused import writes nothing. The verbs refuse while markdown files stand. `resolve` already refuses, changing nothing, while a destination is taken or a source sits behind a symbolic link ([ADMINISTRATION.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md#L169)). It checks neither the index lock nor a folder's write access before its first write.

Sprint certification of [`2026-10-05-issue-dashboard.md`](.ok-planner/history/sprints/2026-10-05-issue-dashboard.md) (run `converge-2026-10-05T045158`, defect i30) tried two fixes, then backed both out:

1. Fix task t18 moved every file first, then imported, and moved the files back where the import refused. Verifier t22 sent it back: "owned-paths check fails on converge:598; rollback move adds a split write on the refused-import path". The move back is a second write that can itself fail, and [checks/owned-paths](checks/owned-paths) did not list the new move call site.
2. Fix task t24 returned to import first, then move, and taught the next `/ok` to offer a move-only resolve for files whose records already stand. It closed partial because [`admin/ADMINISTRATION.md`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md) still described the first fix, and that file lay outside its task. No verifier ruled on its code.

The owner's comment of 2026-10-06 sets the bar: in no event may converge leave the migration incomplete. Where a move cannot happen, converge stops and asks the owner to settle the cause. That rules out a fix that leaves a half-migrated state for the next `/ok` to finish.

Three facts bound a fix. A JSON Lines file and the git index cannot share one transaction, as project rule [plumbline-coding 3.1](.claude/rules/plumbline-coding.md#L30) asks of a change that writes two resources. An import cannot be undone, because the intake format says "Never delete a record" ([artifact-definitions.md](.claude/skills/_shared/artifact-definitions.md#L294)). One `git mv` call given every tracked source takes git's index lock before it renames any file, so a held lock fails the call with nothing moved; a probe confirmed this. A fix that meets the bar therefore checks every cause it can see before its first write, moves the files before the import in one call, and moves them back only on an import failure no check foresaw.

A fix touches [`admin/converge`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge) (`resolve`, `move_path`, the two offers), [`admin/ADMINISTRATION.md`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md) (the offer table, the draft checks, the markdown-intake paragraph, the pre-4.0 tensions paragraph), the intake module for a dry-run import, and [`checks/owned-paths`](checks/owned-paths) for each new move call site.

## Options

The ruling decides how the intake migration ends when a write cannot happen partway.

recommendation.text:
Option A. Before its first write, the `markdown-intake` and `tensions` migration refuses, writing nothing and naming the cause, while `.git/index.lock` exists, a source or destination folder cannot be written, a destination is taken, or the intake module's dry run of the import refuses a record. It then moves every tracked file in one `git mv` call and each untracked file by rename, and imports. Where the import fails after the move, it moves the files back and stops with the cause named. The administration document describes each refusal and the move back.

Rationale: the owner ruled that converge never leaves the migration incomplete, and that it stops and asks where a move cannot happen. The checks turn every cause the core can see into a refusal before any write. That refusal is the stop-and-ask: the agent driving `/ok` shows it, and the owner settles the cause. One `git mv` call moves every tracked file or none, so a lock taken between the check and the call still moves nothing. The files move before the import because an import cannot be undone: the intake format never deletes a record. The dry run removes the refused import that made the first fix's move back routine, the path verifier t22 sent back, and leaves the move back for a failure no check could see. Options B and D leave the half state the owner ruled out. Option C is option A without the checks. The flip case: if a process killed between the move and the import must also end complete, no order of two stores achieves it. The migration would then have to record its pending import so the next `/ok` finishes it, which is option B's resume joined to option A.

ruling.text: Option A

Option 1. Amend story:see-new-analysis to say that any revision of an issue already routed or ruled reaches the owner as new analysis, whichever ceremony writes it. A first routing stays silent. Then make the intake record every such revision as an update message the owner has not read.

Rationale: the story names no writer, and its purpose, "respond to each change without rereading the intake", fails exactly where option 2 leaves the gap: a ruling standing over a problem the owner never saw. decision:triage-answers-owner-messages already holds that a ruled issue stays ruled and its revision reaches the owner as new analysis; option 1 extends that rule to every writer and leaves the decision true as written. Option 3 lets an agent unsettle the owner's ruling, which the intake forbids everywhere else. Scoping to routed or ruled issues keeps a first routing from inflating the unread count. Rule this with its sibling unread-view-lists-closed-issues, which amends the same story. The flip case: if the owner treats a re-filed issue as a fresh question, to be ruled again from scratch rather than read as a change, option 2 is enough for unruled issues, and only the ruled case needs a signal.

options.label: A

A first routing stays silent, since "needs ruling" already surfaces it. Cost: `revise` writes an update message on those issues, and the message needs an author value for a writer other than triage.

options.label: B

options.label: C

problem:
The intake marks a change to an issue as new for the owner only when the change arrives as an update message. One verb of the intake module, `issues respond`, writes that message. Another, `issues revise`, rewrites an issue's fields and writes none. `/converge` uses `revise` to turn a stuck defect issue into a judgment issue, and rewrites its problem. Where the owner had ruled that issue, the ruling now stands over a problem the owner never saw, and nothing flags the change. [story:see-new-analysis](.ok-planner/design/stories/see-new-analysis.md) promises "a way to see which issues have new answers or revisions since I last read them, so that I respond to each change without rereading the intake". [decision:triage-answers-owner-messages](.ok-planner/design/decisions/triage-answers-owner-messages.md) says a revision of a ruled issue "reaches the owner as new analysis", but it speaks of triage alone. Neither says whether a revision by another ceremony counts.

## Mechanism

In [`plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/issues`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/issues), [`revise`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/issues#L600) applies the fields and stamps `updated`. [`respond`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/issues#L641) applies fields too, and also appends a triage `update` message with `read` unset. The unread count counts only those unset messages. So a `respond` raises the count, and a `revise` never does.

Triage routes its re-check of an already routed issue through `respond`, so the decision holds for triage. Three callers use `revise`:

- `/converge`'s owner list, which turns a stuck or left-alone defect issue into a judgment issue: it sets `category`, clears `route` and `recommendation`, and appends a `## Stuck in <run>` or `## Left alone in <run>` section to the problem.
- Triage's first routing of a new issue, and its reuse route.
- Triage's defect route.

After the owner list's revise, an unruled issue shows under "waiting on triage", then under "needs ruling" once triage routes it again. A ruled issue stays "ruled": the module never lets an agent change the owner's ruling, and its state reads the ruling first. The drive in run `converge-2026-10-05T045158` (drive failures i7 and i8, question i25) saw this on the command line and on the dashboard: after `issues read`, a `revise` of the problem "exited 0 ... and 'issues list --unread' did not list it", and "the page's unread count stayed 0; the same held for ruled see-new-analysis-three".

## State of play

Triage's revisions of a routed issue reach the owner. Every other revision does not. For an unruled issue the triage queue still surfaces it. For a ruled issue nothing does.

## Options

The ruling decides whether a revision by a ceremony other than triage reaches the owner as new analysis.

messages.text:
Option 1. Amend story:see-new-analysis to say that an answer on a closed issue counts as new until the owner reads it, and that the place the owner looks for new answers shows it, marked closed.

Rationale: the answer that lands just before a close is often the one that explains the close: why triage answered or retired the issue, or why a run fixed it. The owner acts on that by vetoing or reopening, and decision:closed-issues-leave-the-live-file names the archive as where the veto list lives. Option 2 sends the owner to browse the closed list, the rereading the story exists to spare. Option 3 hides that answer or holds every close on the owner. options.label: A
options.text: **Closed answers count.** An answer on a closed issue counts as new until the owner reads it, wherever the owner looks for new answers (the code as built). Cost: the unread view mixes closed issues with open ones, so it must mark each closed one as closed.

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: **Closing settles the answer.** Closing an issue marks its answers read, or a closer may not close an issue with an unread answer. Cost: the owner never sees the last answer as new, or every close waits on the owner.

problem:
Triage may answer an owner's comment and then close the issue in the same run, so the answer can land on a record that is already closed. A fixer in sprint certification of [`2026-10-05-issue-dashboard.md`](.ok-planner/history/sprints/2026-10-05-issue-dashboard.md) (run `converge-2026-10-05T045158`, defect i23) chose to show such answers in the unread view: `issues list --unread`, `GET /api/issues?unread=1`, and the dashboard's unread tab now list closed issues beside open ones. [story:see-new-analysis](.ok-planner/design/stories/see-new-analysis.md) promises "a way to see which issues have new answers or revisions since I last read them, so that I respond to each change without rereading the intake". It says nothing about closed issues. The fixer recorded the choice as question i39 and built the inclusive reading.

## Mechanism

A triage reply or update on an issue is stored unread. A later close, by triage's answered route, `/converge`'s owner list, or a sprint promotion, moves the record to the archive file with that message still unread. [decision:closed-issues-leave-the-live-file](.ok-planner/design/decisions/closed-issues-leave-the-live-file.md) sets where the record sits, not what the unread view lists.

In [`plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/issues`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/issues), [`select`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/issues#L450) builds the unread pool from the live records plus the archived ones. The dashboard's unread route calls the same function. `issues read` and the dashboard's read route mark a closed record's answers read through a lookup that searches the archive too. Before the fix, the answer stood only in the archive: the unread view never named it, `issues read` refused the closed record, and the closed tab showed it as new forever. The drive that confirmed the fix found "answered-then-closed issues listed by 'issues list --unread', GET /api/issues?unread=1, and the page's unread tab".

## State of play

The stuck read state is fixed. An owner can read a closed answer and clear it. What remains open is only whether the unread view is the place that answer shows.

## Options

The ruling decides whether the unread view lists closed issues.

messages.text: Held out of sprint 2026-10-06 (intake drain). We don't understand how requiring process ids for ports wouldn't be a burden on whatever is starting those processes. We don't know all the process types that a project or stack might need to run and don't understand how that approach wouldn't be fragile later. There are a huge number of ports, and we can know if a lease is stuck by grace of the project no longer running any ad hoc stacks. And the implementation should be project local, not a global registry. Each project should be configurable with a range, then allocate ports only there. Unless projects are running a huge number of parallel tests or drivers, a few hundred (or even dozen) ports should suffice.

You are right about option C, and its cost line understated the problem. A process id check is fragile beyond the work of writing it: a server started through a wrapper (an npm script, a shell script, a process manager) reports the wrapper's id, not the listener's; a container's id belongs to another namespace; and the operating system reuses ids, so an unrelated live process can pass. I rewrote C's cost to say so.

Your direction is an option the analysis missed, and I added it as option D with a recommended ruling for it. It works against this issue's harm because the harm needs the operating system to hand a freed port to the next run. Today every stack binds port 0, so the operating system picks from its ephemeral range (49152 to 65535 here) and nothing keeps a freed port away from the next run. Under a project-local lease, a stopped server's port stays leased to its run, so that run's readback hits a port nothing listens on and fails, instead of passing against another run's server. A stuck lease fails safe: it wastes one port until you clear the leases while no stack runs, as you say.

Two points the ruling should settle. First, the current decision's Rationale rejects every allocator because a program outside the scheme can bind a port between the lease and the stack's bind. Placing the range below the ephemeral range narrows that to a program that binds a fixed port in the range, and such a collision fails the stack's bind loudly. Second, a lease store in one checkout is invisible to another checkout of the same project, so concurrent runs from two worktrees would share a range unless the store sits where every worktree reads it, such as the git common directory.

Revised after the owner's comment. problem: added a section, Why the port goes to another run, explaining that the harm depends on the operating system reassigning a freed port and that a project-local lease removes that condition; reframed the closing Options line around OS-assigned ports versus a project-local range; corrected the ADMINISTRATION.md link from line 159 to line 160. options: rewrote A to drop the misplaced claim about allocators; rewrote C's cost to name the fragility the owner raised (wrappers, container namespaces, reused process ids); added D, a project-local port range with leases, with its cost against the decision's Rationale. recommendation: added a recommended ruling for D, with the worktree case as its flip.

Replace the read-back with a project-local port registry. The project's configuration lists the host ports its stack expects, by name. The operator chooses each project's range below the ephemeral range at setup, and gives each project its own range. When a run starts its stack, the tool atomically leases a free batch from the range, skips any port another program already holds, writes the lease to a registry in the project's cache, and passes the ports to the stack's environment. The services do nothing special. A compose file names each host port with a variable and a default, such as `"${WEB_PORT:-8080}:8080"`. A server outside compose takes its port from the environment or a flag. A bind failure is loud, and the run retries with a fresh batch. Leases end when the run's stack goes down. A cleanup step, run periodically (after a sprint's batch of drives, for example), frees each lease whose port nothing holds and whose compose project has no containers left. Worktrees are out of scope: the registry serves the one checkout.

A cleanup step, run periodically (after a sprint's batch of drives, for example), frees each lease whose port nothing holds and whose compose project has no containers left. Worktrees are out of scope: the registry serves the one checkout.

The suite bakes this in as one of its own opinionated rules, not a project practice. The rule goes in the suite's coding rules, so /converge fixes a break of it under A8, and the ok-planner cheatsheet's section on per-run artifacts and verification stacks is rewritten to match. The rule says: use the suite's lint where it applies, and/or a project-specific lint, that checks at least that (1) every host port a stack definition publishes comes from an environment variable with a fallback, never a bare number; (2) each variable's name is a port name the project declares in .ok-planner/config.json; (3) no fallback falls inside the project's provisioning range. The suite's lint gains this check for compose files. Like the other lint checks, it is on by default and off only where lint_checks sets it to false, and the rules text for it leaves the rules files when it is off. The project's own lint, where it has one, also covers the suite's other rules: no prose comments, every citation resolves, and no test edits.

Converge walks the owner through the range. Where a project publishes ports (names under ports in its config, or a compose file that publishes a port) and declares no range, the converge core prints a cleanup offer that needs the owner's choice. It names the ports it found and suggests a range picked at random above 1024 and below 49152, clear of every well-known port, which no listening program holds at that moment. /ok asks once: take the suggestion or name another range. It refuses a range at or above 49152, and reminds the owner that no other project on the machine may share the range, since no project can see another's registry. On the answer, the core's amend mode writes the range and the port names into .ok-planner/config.json. A declined offer comes back on the next /ok. Until the project has a range, the allocator refuses to run and says to run /ok. A project that publishes no ports gets no question.

A provisioning range stays clear of well-known ports. The suite carries its own list of the standard ports that protocols, apps, and services use by default, including popular defaults that no registry lists, such as 4200, 5173, 6379, and 27017. Where the machine has a services database, such as /etc/services, the core also avoids every port it lists. The two sources are also the allocator's block list: it never leases a listed port, so a range may span listed ports and simply skips them. The random suggestion still falls in a gap that neither source touches, so every port in it can be leased. Where the owner names a range that overlaps listed ports, /ok warns: it names the ports it hits and how many of the range's ports remain to lease, and the owner may keep the range or pick another.

On Linux, a range /ok accepts between 32768 and 49151 shares ports the operating system hands to port-0 binds, so reading the bound from the machine keeps the ruling's own rule that the range lies below the ephemeral range.

problem:
`port-block` tells a verification run which host ports its own stack got. It handles two kinds of entry. A service entry names a container. When no container of that service runs, `port-block` refuses. A record entry names a file a dev server wrote its port to. `port-block` prints that port with exit 0 whether or not the server still runs. The story [concurrent-stacks-without-port-collisions](.ok-planner/design/stories/concurrent-stacks-without-port-collisions.md) promises that one verification run never disturbs another's results. A stale record can break that promise.

## How it happens

A dev server listens on port 0, the operating system hands it a free port, and the server writes that port to a file whose path holds the run tag. `port-block <run-tag>` later reads the file back ([`plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/port-block`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/port-block), [`recorded_port`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/port-block#L142-L150)). It refuses only when the file is missing or holds no port number. [`ADMINISTRATION.md`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md#L160) describes the record entry and says nothing about who removes the file.

The file outlives its server unless something deletes it. A run tag is unique to one run, so a later run never reads an earlier run's file. The harm falls inside one run: its server stops or crashes, the operating system gives the freed port to another run's server, and the first run reads its record back and verifies against the other run's server. The run sees a passing result that belongs to someone else.

Evidence, from drive failure i28 in sprint certification run converge-2026-10-04T060800: after run B's dev server stopped, `port-block run-1d45e73b9246` printed `DB_PORT=55058` and `WEB_PORT=55061` and exited 0, and `curl -s -m 2 localhost:55061` exited 7, connection refused. After run A's compose stack went down, its service entry refused: `no running container of service db in compose project run-7478b68995b5`, exit 1.

## What the corpus says

The decision [os-assigned-ports-read-back-by-run-tag](.ok-planner/design/decisions/os-assigned-ports-read-back-by-run-tag.md) says `port-block` "reads back, by that tag, the host ports the stack got". It also says that where a stack cannot bind this way, "the project's own stack commands handle isolation". The concept [run-tag](.ok-planner/design/concepts/run-tag.md) says wiring the tag into stacks is the project's own change. Neither says what happens to a record whose server has stopped. If the decision promises a live readback, the accept list's entry for a false report someone acts on ([A9](.ok-planner/review/catalog/accept.md#L17)) covers this, and it is a defect.

## Why the port goes to another run

The harm needs two things: a freed port, and an operating system that hands it to the next server that asks. Under the decision every stack binds port 0, so the operating system picks from its whole ephemeral range (49152 to 65535 on this machine, by `sysctl net.inet.ip.portrange`), and nothing keeps a freed port away from the next run. Options A to C keep port 0 and try to detect the stale record afterward. Option D, the owner's direction, removes the second condition: the project hands out ports from a range it owns, and a port leased to one run goes to no other run until that lease ends. A run whose server has stopped then reads back a port nothing listens on, and its checks fail with connection refused instead of passing against someone else's server.

## Options

The ruling decides whether ports stay OS-assigned with a check on the readback, or come from a project-local range by lease.

It names the ports it found and suggests a range picked at random above 1024 and below the start of the machine's ephemeral range, clear of every well-known port, which no listening program holds at that moment. /ok asks once: take the suggestion or name another range. It reads where the ephemeral range starts from the machine (sysctl net.inet.ip.portrange.first on macOS, /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_local_port_range on Linux), and uses 49152 where it cannot read the value. It refuses a range that reaches that start, and reminds the owner that no other project on the machine may share the range, since no project can see another's registry. On the answer, the core's amend mode writes the range and the port names into .ok-planner/config.json. A declined offer comes back on the next /ok. Until the project has a range, the allocator refuses to run and says to run /ok. A project that publishes no ports gets no question.

A provisioning range stays clear of well-known ports. The suite carries its own list of the standard ports that protocols, apps, and services use by default, including popular defaults that no registry lists, such as 4200, 5173, 6379, and 27017. Where the machine has a services database, such as /etc/services, the core also avoids every port it lists. The two sources are also the allocator's block list: it never leases a listed port, so a range may span listed ports and simply skips them. The random suggestion still falls in a gap that neither source touches, so every port in it can be leased. Where the owner names a range that overlaps listed ports, /ok warns: it names the ports it hits and how many of the range's ports remain to lease, and the owner may keep the range or pick another.

title: port-block prints a dev server's recorded port after that server has stopped

Rationale: B is the only option that gives each act one name, which the concept template and the writing standard's "use the same term for the same thing every time" both ask for, without breaking a verb that crosses the release boundary as C does. A records the double name rather than resolving it, so the concept's vocabulary reading keeps failing and the issue returns at each audit. B's reach is wide but mechanical, and everything it touches outside the corpus is suite-owned and rewritten whole on the next `/ok`. Flip case: if the owner judges the rename's reach larger than the harm of an ambiguity readers have so far resolved from context, A is the cheap holding answer, taken knowing the template's issue stays open.

options.label: A
options.text: Record "converge" as an alias of true-up, and say in the concept's Boundaries that the `/converge` command is a different act. Cost: one live word still names two acts, and the template's two-names issue stands at every audit.

options.label: B
options.text: Use "true-up" alone for the administration act in the corpus, the suite's documents, the core and its mode, and the stamp wording, and keep "converge" for the `/converge` defect run. Cost: a rewrite of about 60 corpus sentences, the integration contract, the administration document, and the core, and a new stamp line in every suite-owned file on the next `/ok`.

options.label: C
options.text: Rename the `/converge` command so "converge" names only the administration act. Cost: it renames a slash verb that crosses the release boundary, which every owner and every sprint's closing step (`/converge sprint <path>`) calls.

problem:
The corpus uses "converge" both for the suite's administration act, which [concept:true-up](.ok-planner/design/concepts/true-up.md) defines, and for the `/converge` command, the defect run, a different act. That breaks the concept template's rule that a concept has one live name, and a reader cannot tell from the word alone which act a sentence means.

The mechanism. [concept:true-up](.ok-planner/design/concepts/true-up.md) calls the act "the idempotent converge of a project's suite presence" and says "Which content converge may move or write without asking is the ownership rule's", and it has no Aliases section. The front door's core that performs the act is the file [`admin/converge`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge), run in a mode named converge, and the stamp line on every suite-owned file reads "overwritten on converge". The ruling decides which act keeps the word "converge".

problem:
Site: [implementation-auditor.md:coverage auditor Method step 1](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_shared/implementation-auditor.md#L499-L504) and [implementation-auditor.md:reading auditor quantifier step](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_shared/implementation-auditor.md#L117-L122), with [audit/SKILL.md:task prompt resolution](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/audit/SKILL.md#L132), which writes those prompts into the run's task bodies and tells them no folder.

Entry: [A8](.ok-planner/review/catalog/accept.md#L16), through [decision:project-declares-its-folders](.ok-planner/design/decisions/project-declares-its-folders.md): "Every tool that lists or scopes the project's code reads that list." [story:project-spans-folders](.ok-planner/design/stories/project-spans-folders.md) owes the same: "so that no check the suite runs over my project misses code I own."

Trigger: a project declares `folders` in `.ok-planner/config.json` and keeps code that a subject's population or a quantified claim covers in one of those folders.

Harm: the coverage auditor and the reading auditor enumerate a population from the project root alone, so a member under a declared folder is never counted, and a practice violation there is never filed. The audit's `checked:` count then reports coverage it did not measure.

Evidence: [implementation-auditor.md#L501](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_shared/implementation-auditor.md#L501) says only "Enumerate from the codebase", and [implementation-auditor.md#L118](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_shared/implementation-auditor.md#L118) only "enumerate the population from reality". A search for `folders` under plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills hits only [converge/SKILL.md#L36](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/SKILL.md#L36), [converge/SKILL.md#L53](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/SKILL.md#L53), [audit/SKILL.md#L99](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/audit/SKILL.md#L99) (the surface extractor), and [audit/SKILL.md#L204](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/audit/SKILL.md#L204) (the lint sweep). The auditor prompts never read the list.

A merge agent confirmed it in run converge-2026-10-06T034157 (drive failure i8). The files stand unchanged since base 1ff2a91, so the defect lies outside sprint 2026-10-05-second-intake-drain.

recommendation.text: Fix [plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_shared/implementation-auditor.md:coverage auditor Method step 1](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_shared/implementation-auditor.md#L499-L504) and [reading auditor quantifier step](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_shared/implementation-auditor.md#L117-L122), and [plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/audit/SKILL.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/audit/SKILL.md#L132) where it resolves those prompts, so the auditors enumerate each folder `.ok-planner/config.json` declares under `folders` and no population member under a declared folder goes uncounted.

title: The audit's coverage and reading auditors never learn the folders the project declares beside its root

problem:
Sites: [converge:strip_story_sections](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L3069-L3086) and [converge:strip_decision_proofs](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L3089-L3099), which the core's `corpus` mode runs on every `/ok` with no question. [ADMINISTRATION.md#L201](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md#L201) and [ADMINISTRATION.md#L371](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md#L371) describe the same behavior.

Entries: [A2](.ok-planner/review/catalog/accept.md#L10), a delete or an overwrite reaches something it should not: cleanup reaches an owner's untracked concept file the suite did not create, and owner text git holds no copy of. [A8](.ok-planner/review/catalog/accept.md#L16), through [decision:whole-file-ownership](.ok-planner/design/decisions/whole-file-ownership.md): the machinery "never edits a file a human also edits, save the one removal of a retired family's unread state file and the rewrites of references to retired suite paths", and even that removal sends "an uncommitted or symlinked one ... to the owner like any other estate edit". [story:converge-project-estate](.ok-planner/design/stories/converge-project-estate.md) owes the owner "that upgrading the suite never costs me work I wrote."

Trigger: an owner holds uncommitted or untracked text in a story's `## Falsifier`, `## Proof`, or `## Acceptance` section or a decision's `## Proof` section, or keeps an untracked concept of their own at `design/concepts/falsifier.md`, and runs `/ok`.

Harm: the strip deletes the section text and collapses blank-line runs across the whole file, and the core removes the concept file, with no check of git status. Text git cannot recover is lost.

Evidence: [converge#L3073](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L3073) `new = re.sub(r"\n## (Falsifier|Proof|Acceptance)\n.*?(?=\n## |\Z)", "\n", text, flags=re.S)`, [converge#L3074](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L3074) `new = re.sub(r"\n{3,}", "\n\n", new)`, [converge#L3080-L3081](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L3080-L3081) `if os.path.exists(concept):` then `os.remove(concept)`, and [converge#L3093](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L3093) for decisions; neither function reads git. In the drive of the story, the driver's untracked `use-go.md` lost its Proof prose, and its untracked `concepts/falsifier.md` was removed ("Retired story sections eliminated: removed: concepts/falsifier.md").

A merge agent confirmed it in run converge-2026-10-06T034157 (drive failures i9 and i10, one defect). Both functions are byte-identical to base 1ff2a91, so the defect lies outside sprint 2026-10-05-second-intake-drain.

recommendation.text: Fix [plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge:strip_story_sections](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L3069-L3086) and [:strip_decision_proofs](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L3089-L3099), with the matching text in [plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md#L201), so an uncommitted, untracked, or symlinked story, decision, or falsifier concept goes to the owner as an estate edit offer and no owner text git cannot recover is rewritten or removed.

title: Converge strips uncommitted story and decision text, and removes an owner's falsifier concept, beyond recovery

problem:
Site: [ADMINISTRATION.md:"Audit the project against the carried version"](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md#L238-L260), the `.claude/settings.json` row of the "What it reads" table.

Entry: [A9](.ok-planner/review/catalog/accept.md#L17), the system reports something false that someone acts on.

Trigger: a `.claude/settings.json` hook entry whose command calls a script the carried version materializes under `.ok-planner/bin/`, such as `.ok-planner/bin/run-tag` or `.ok-planner/bin/plumbline`. The converge core writes such an entry itself when it repoints a hook that named a retired script: [ADMINISTRATION.md:"Callers of retired suite scripts"](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md#L228) names `.ok-planner/bin/plumbline`, `.ok-planner/bin/catalog-toc`, and `.ok-planner/bin/run-tag` as the drop-ins it repoints to.

Harm: the audit's report line tells the owner that a working hook names something the carried version replaced, and the owner acts on it by rewording a valid hook. The report line also leaves the finding pending, so `/ok`'s outcome does not read `converged` on a project that is converged.

Evidence: [ADMINISTRATION.md:249](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md#L249) makes a finding of "an entry whose command names a path under `.ok-planner/`, `.claude/hooks/`, `.ok-plumbline/`, or `.ok-workspaces/` that the table does not list and the `lint` group's command does not remove", and the wiring table it reads against ([ADMINISTRATION.md:44-49](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md#L44-L49)) lists only the hook scripts, never `bin/`. [ADMINISTRATION.md:258](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md#L258) sorts a `.claude/settings.json` entry outside the wiring table as a report line the owner rewords, and [ADMINISTRATION.md:260](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md#L260) says a report line leaves its finding pending and "`/ok`'s outcome reads `converged` only when none is pending". The executables the core materializes, `bin/run-tag` and `bin/plumbline` among them, are listed at [ADMINISTRATION.md:28](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md#L28).

A fixer noticed this in run converge-2026-10-06T034157 (call i44); triage re-verified it against the document as it stands.

recommendation.text: Fix [ADMINISTRATION.md:"Audit the project against the carried version"](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md#L249) so a `.claude/settings.json` hook entry naming a path the carried version still materializes is no finding, and the audit no longer reports a valid hook as a line to reword.

title: The front door's project audit tells the owner to reword a settings hook that calls a live estate script

messages.text:
A dashboard drive builds the page from the tree's source into scratch space outside the tree, and the scratch project serves that build in place of the committed release build, stamped with the suite version the way converge stamps the placed build. The drive then certifies the page the sprint changed, and the committed build stays a release artifact.

Rationale: A is the one option that drives the sprint's real page and keeps both standing decisions. [decision:pinned-build-placed-at-converge](.ok-planner/design/decisions/pinned-build-placed-at-converge.md) keeps its build once per release, because the drive's build lives and dies in scratch space. [decision:drive-tries-each-story-as-a-user](.ok-planner/design/decisions/drive-tries-each-story-as-a-user.md) keeps its rule that a driver writes nothing in the project tree. B reverses the first decision to serve a test need and commits a churning bundle with every page sprint. C and D give up the page coverage certification exists to provide; D only relabels the failure. The repeated build steps are a few commands in the owner's drive facts, a small price for a drive that sees what will ship. Flip case: if the machines that run certification cannot count on node and network access for `npm ci`, a build-from-source drive fails on environment every time, and D becomes the better call, since it names the gap without spending a fixer.

problem.after:
Sprint certification's dashboard drive serves the page build the last release committed, so a sprint that changes the page source is driven against the old page and fails on a change no fixer can act on. That defeats the drive's job under [decision:drive-tries-each-story-as-a-user](.ok-planner/design/decisions/drive-tries-each-story-as-a-user.md): to try each story the sprint adds or amends on the running product.

The mechanism. The drive commands in [.ok-planner/review/project.md](.ok-planner/review/project.md#L43) build a scratch project by running the converge core. The core copies the committed bundle at `browser/dist/` into the scratch project's `.ok-planner/dashboard/` ([converge:BUILD_SRC](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L252-L253)) and stamps the suite version into it. Only the release skill's step 5a ([.claude/skills/release/SKILL.md](.claude/skills/release/SKILL.md#L129-L149)) runs `npm ci` and `npm run build`, as [decision:pinned-build-placed-at-converge](.ok-planner/design/decisions/pinned-build-placed-at-converge.md) requires: the page is built once per suite release and carried as payload. Between releases, `browser/src/` moves and `browser/dist/` does not. When run converge-2026-10-06T034157 drove, `browser/dist/` dated from release v25.3.0 (1ff2a91), while the sprint under certification had changed [`browser/src/lib/api.js`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/browser/src/lib/api.js), [`browser/src/lib/markdown.js`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/browser/src/lib/markdown.js), and [`browser/src/views/IssueDetail.svelte`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/browser/src/views/IssueDetail.svelte). Release v25.4.0 (4855d1e) has since rebuilt `browser/dist/`, so the two agree today, and the gap opens again with the next sprint that changes the page source.

The state of play. In run converge-2026-10-06T034157, the driver of [story:see-new-analysis](.ok-planner/design/stories/see-new-analysis.md) drove the pre-sprint page and failed. The merge agent read the page source instead and found it right, so the run spent a drive on a failure with nothing to fix. A driver writes nothing in the project tree, so it cannot rebuild `browser/dist/` itself; it may write in a scratch project. The corpus says nothing about how a drive obtains a page build.

The ruling decides where a dashboard drive gets the page it drives when the tree's page source is newer than the committed build.

problem:

Only the readable `show` leaves the difference out, and it did so before the latest sprint too. No accept-list entry names this as a defect.
