problem.after:
The converge core rewrites lines in discover-design's notes under `.ok-planner/design/_discover/`, which record what a discovery run observed, and [decision:whole-file-ownership](.ok-planner/design/decisions/whole-file-ownership.md) forbids rewriting a record: "A record states what was true when it was written, so rewriting one to match a current layout destroys the only thing it is for." The corpus already marks the notes as point-in-time: [concept:design-corpus](.ok-planner/design/concepts/design-corpus.md) says "The discovery scaffold is point-in-time and exempt from the durable rules", and the owner's ruling names them records. Accept-list entry A8 covers the harm: a live artifact's commitment decides the fix.

The mechanism. [converge:repoint_callers](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L1804) rewrites a line wherever [converge:script_pattern](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L1656) matches a retired suite script's path. [converge:caller_kind](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L1691) skips a file only where [review:left_alone](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/review#L198) answers record or suite, plus the rules file and the memory file. left_alone answers with the first class in [review:OWNER_PATHS](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/review#L45-L62) whose prefix matches, and the corpus class lists all of `.ok-planner/design/`, so every `_discover/` note reads as corpus. caller_kind also decides which files count as callers, so a note that names a retired script keeps converge from removing that script, and draws an intake issue where the script has no drop-in.

The state of play. In this repository the harm already happened: a converge rewrote the retired lint path in the note now at [history/discover/script-materialization.md](.ok-planner/history/discover/script-materialization.md#L12) and filed an issue about [history/discover/src-tag.md](.ok-planner/history/discover/src-tag.md#L14). The owner put the line back and moved the notes to `.ok-planner/history/discover/` by hand on 2026-10-13, where OWNER_PATHS already classes them as record. The code is unchanged, so every project that keeps its notes under `_discover/` meets the same rewrite at its next `/ok`. The sibling issue discover-design-offers-to-archive-its-notes asks whether discover-design should offer that move, and retired-script-reference-root-prefix-unsettled asks about the repoint's scope behind a root prefix. The filed concern about migration documentation does not hold: no document in the tree names a full retired script path.

The fix classes the notes as records, so converge leaves their lines and counts none of them as a caller.

messages.text: option A

Several people may work one project's intake. Every person's comment and ruling records its author's name: the name the user configures, kept with the user and never in the committed project configuration, or else git's user.name. Where neither gives a name, the write refuses and says how to set one. Anyone may comment and anyone may rule; the latest ruling stands.

The dashboard picks a message's style from its type, not its author: comments and rulings are a person's, replies and updates an agent's. It shows the author's name on every message. A name it does not know is a person.

Read marks move out of the committed intake into a per-user ledger under .ok-planner/.cache/, which git ignores, so opening an issue changes no committed file. Each person's unread counts come from their own ledger. A fresh ledger, in a new clone or on a person's first run, starts with everything that exists counted as read. Triage's seen mark on a person's message stays in the committed record, so every clone agrees on which messages triage has answered. This also settles new-issues-show-no-unread-mark's question of how existing issues count: they count as read when the ledger starts.

after.label: A
after.text: One owner works the intake, as built: comments and rulings carry `owner`, a message by any other author shows in agent styling under its raw author with no "new" tag, and read marks stay in the committed record. Cost: a second person's words carry no name, and one person's reading clears every other person's unread marks.

after.label: B
after.text: Several people work the intake. Each comment and ruling records its author's name, from a setting kept with the user or else git's user.name, and the write refuses where neither gives one. The dashboard picks a message's style from its type and shows every author's name. Read marks move into a per-user ledger under `.ok-planner/.cache/` that git ignores, which starts with everything read, and triage's seen mark stays in the committed record. Cost: a change to the message schema, the module's author check, the dashboard's styling, and where the unread count reads its marks.

after.label: C
after.text: Several people work the intake and every message records its author's name as in B, but read marks stay in the committed record, kept per person by name. Cost: opening an issue still changes a committed file, and every person's reading lands in every clone's history.

after.label: D
after.text: One owner works the intake, and a message whose author is neither the owner nor a known agent shows under a third style labelled as from an unknown author. Cost: one more display branch, and the intake still has no place for a second person.

before.label: A

before.label: B

before.label: C
before.text: The corpus commits that only a known agent's message shows in agent styling, and every other message shows as the owner's. Cost: an unknown author's message is labelled "you" and "not yet seen by triage", a false status.

problem.after:
The intake and its dashboard assume one person works an issue. Every comment and ruling is written as `owner`, the dashboard picks a message's style from its author, and reading an issue writes read marks into the committed record. Several people may work one project's intake, and no corpus artifact says how a second person's messages and reading are recorded or shown. [decision:agent-revisions-reach-the-owner](.ok-planner/design/decisions/agent-revisions-reach-the-owner.md) and [story:see-new-analysis](.ok-planner/design/stories/see-new-analysis.md) promise that new analysis reaches the owner as unread; neither says whose reading clears it when several people read.

The mechanism. The intake module accepts a comment or ruling only from `owner`, and a reply or update only from `triage-issues` or `converge` ([issues:AUTHORS](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/issues#L57)), so no write records which person spoke. On read, [decision:intake-reads-past-stray-lines](.ok-planner/design/decisions/intake-reads-past-stray-lines.md) keeps a record whose old message breaks the schema, and [issues:readable_message](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/issues#L295-L301) gives a `seen` mark only to a message by `owner`. The dashboard's [api.js:isAgent](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/browser/src/lib/api.js#L81) reads `message.by !== OWNER`, so [IssueDetail.svelte](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/browser/src/views/IssueDetail.svelte#L223-L241) shows every other author in agent styling: a person's message under any name but `owner`, from a hand edit or an earlier layout, looks like an agent's analysis. [api.js:isNew](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/browser/src/lib/api.js#L76) gives the "new" tag only to an unread message from `triage-issues` or `converge`. Reading an issue, through `issues read` or the dashboard, stamps `read` on its agent messages in `.ok-planner/issues.jsonl` itself ([issues:mark_read](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/issues#L921)). So opening an issue changes a committed file, and once that change is committed it clears the unread mark for every other person who pulls it.

The state of play. For a single owner the build states nothing false: it names a message's raw author and claims no unread status for an unknown one. With several people, three things break. A person's message cannot carry that person's name. A message carrying a person's name shows as an agent's. Each person's unread counts follow whoever read last, and the reading lands in git's history. The issue new-issues-show-no-unread-mark asks how an issue never opened counts as unread, and its answer turns on how existing issues count when per-person reading starts.

The ruling decides how the intake records and shows the messages and the reading of several people.
problem.before:

[decision:agent-revisions-reach-the-owner](.ok-planner/design/decisions/agent-revisions-reach-the-owner.md) and [story:see-new-analysis](.ok-planner/design/stories/see-new-analysis.md) cover agent messages reaching the owner as unread; neither covers a message whose author is unknown.

The mechanism. The intake module checks a message's author only when it writes the message ([issues:one_message_defects](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/issues#L177)): a comment or ruling must come from `owner`, a reply or update from `triage-issues` or `converge`. On read, [decision:intake-reads-past-stray-lines](.ok-planner/design/decisions/intake-reads-past-stray-lines.md) keeps a record whose old message breaks the schema, and [issues:readable_message](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/issues#L295-L301) turns a missing or non-text author into an empty one. So a hand-edited message, or one written by an earlier layout, can reach the dashboard with any author. Only such a message is affected. The dashboard's [api.js:isAgent](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/browser/src/lib/api.js#L81) reads `message.by !== OWNER`, so [IssueDetail.svelte](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/browser/src/views/IssueDetail.svelte#L223-L241) shows the message in agent styling under its raw author. The unknown-author message therefore never carries a "new" tag the owner could not clear.

The state of play. As built, the page states nothing false about such a message: it names the raw author and claims no unread status. Its styling alone suggests an agent wrote it. The sprint's implementation notes asked to narrow isAgent to the two agent authors as well; that would move the message to the owner's branch, labelled "you" and "not yet seen by triage", a false status the owner may act on ([accept-list](.ok-planner/review/catalog/accept.md) entry A9's kind of harm). The build kept isAgent as it stands.

The ruling decides how the dashboard shows a message whose author is neither the owner nor a known agent.

problem:
The intake and its dashboard assume one person works an issue. Every comment and ruling is written as `owner`, the dashboard picks a message's style from its author, and reading an issue writes read marks into the committed record. Several people may work one project's intake, and no corpus artifact says how a second person's messages and reading are recorded or shown. [decision:agent-revisions-reach-the-owner](.ok-planner/design/decisions/agent-revisions-reach-the-owner.md) and [story:see-new-analysis](.ok-planner/design/stories/see-new-analysis.md) promise that new analysis reaches the owner as unread; neither says whose reading clears it when several people read.

The mechanism. The intake module accepts a comment or ruling only from `owner`, and a reply or update only from `triage-issues` or `converge` ([issues:AUTHORS](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/issues#L57)), so no write records which person spoke. On read, [decision:intake-reads-past-stray-lines](.ok-planner/design/decisions/intake-reads-past-stray-lines.md) keeps a record whose old message breaks the schema, and [issues:readable_message](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/issues#L295-L301) gives a `seen` mark only to a message by `owner`. The dashboard's [api.js:isAgent](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/browser/src/lib/api.js#L81) reads `message.by !== OWNER`, so [IssueDetail.svelte](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/browser/src/views/IssueDetail.svelte#L223-L241) shows every other author in agent styling: a person's message under any name but `owner`, from a hand edit or an earlier layout, looks like an agent's analysis. messages.text:
Converge repoints a retired script reference only where its prefix names the project root with certainty, and counts as certain both the fixed root forms and any prefix it can prove resolves to the root, such as git's top-level idiom when the project root is the repository's top. A reference whose prefix may name the root but cannot be proven to stays as written: converge files an intake issue naming the line and keeps the retired copy, because that line still names it. A path built at run time is outside what converge can see, and its report says so when it removes a copy.

Rationale: this is option D, which keeps option A's guarantee and narrows its cost. The decision already says a caller whose behavior would change reaches the owner as an issue rather than as unrecorded work, and that the suite never edits human work beyond the retired-path exception; option B breaks the second by rewriting lines that may name another file, and option C breaks the first by letting a caller fail. Option A alone files an issue for a prefix converge could have settled, and the decision's rejected alternatives show the project wants no extra question on a migrated project's first converge where the answer is certain. The flip case: if projects whose root sits below their repository's top turn out to be common, the git idiom proves nothing in most of them, and option A alone is the simpler commitment.

options.label: A
options.text: The corpus commits to the built rule: converge repoints a reference only where its prefix certainly names the project root, files an intake issue and keeps the retired copy for a reference whose prefix may name it, and does not see a path built in code. Cost: a retired copy can stay indefinitely until the owner edits the line, and a code-built caller still breaks when the copy goes.

options.label: B
options.text: The corpus commits that converge repoints every reference whose prefix may name the project root, and names each rewrite in its report. Cost: a line about a home or sibling-repository script can be rewritten wrongly, with only a report line as warning.

options.label: C
options.text: The corpus commits that converge leaves an uncertain reference unrewritten, removes the retired copy anyway, and names the line in its report. Cost: a real caller fails at its next run.

options.label: D
options.text: The corpus commits to the rule in A, and also counts as certain a prefix converge can prove resolves to the project root, such as git's top-level idiom where the root is the repository's top. Cost: converge must check that proof on each run, and one more recognized form to maintain.

problem:
When converge migrates a project off a retired suite script, it cannot always tell from a line's text whether the line names the project's retired copy, and the corpus does not say what counts as naming it. [decision:whole-file-ownership](.ok-planner/design/decisions/whole-file-ownership.md) commits converge to rewrite a line in a tracked project file that names a retired suite script's path, and to remove the retired script once no tracked file other than a record names it. It is silent on a line whose path may or may not start at the project root.

The mechanism. A retired script sits either under a retired estate directory (`.ok-plumbline/`, `.ok-workspaces/`, `.ok-review/`, listed in [converge:RETIRED_TOPS](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L1614)) or at a project path such as `bin/run-tag`. An estate directory's name belongs to the suite alone, so [converge:script_pattern](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L1656-L1663) repoints it behind any prefix. A project path like `bin/run-tag` is common, so converge treats it as certainly the project's copy only behind a line start, `./`, the root's absolute path, or `$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR/` in its braced and quoted forms ([converge:ROOT_REFERENCES](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L1617-L1618)). Behind any other prefix that may resolve to the root, such as `$ROOT/bin/run-tag`, `$HOME/bin/run-tag`, `~/bin/run-tag`, `../bin/run-tag`, or `$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)/bin/run-tag`, [converge:may_name_root](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L1666-L1675) and [converge:unsure_reference](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L1678-L1683) mark the reference unsure. Converge then leaves the line as written, files an intake issue for the owner, and keeps the retired copy. A prefix that cannot be the root, such as `/usr/local/`, is ignored, and so is a path a program assembles at run time, which no text search sees. Text alone cannot decide whether `$ROOT` or `~` is the project root, so every rule trades a missed caller against a wrong rewrite. A missed caller meets "not found" at its next run once the copy goes ([accept-list](.ok-planner/review/catalog/accept.md) entry [A3](.ok-planner/review/catalog/accept.md#L11)'s kind of harm). A wrong rewrite points a line about some other file, such as a home script, at the suite's copy (entry [A2](.ok-planner/review/catalog/accept.md#L10)'s kind).

The state of play. Neither harm follows today: the built rule rewrites only certain references and holds the copy behind every uncertain one. Two gaps remain. A retired copy stays as long as an uncertain line names it, until the owner edits that line. A caller that builds the path in code goes unseen, and breaks once the copy goes. The sibling issue converge-repoints-observation-notes-and-migration-docs asks a neighboring question about which tracked files converge rewrites.

The ruling decides which references to a retired script converge repoints, which it leaves to the owner, and whether an uncertain one holds the retired copy.

Flip case: if a later triage routes a question on a case where the corpus decides a file's class in words it can quote, triage needs A's line too.

problem:
Converge's merge prompt sends a report to the owner whenever the review script classes a file of the fix as corpus, even where the corpus itself decides the file's class and the script's list is what departs. [decision:runs-fix-what-the-project-owns](.ok-planner/design/decisions/runs-fix-what-the-project-owns.md) says a run fixes "a clear defect in every file the project owns", and that filing one "spends the owner's attention on a fix the rules already decide".

The mechanism. Before it merges a report, the merge runs an ownership test: `review owner` prints one kind per file, and a `corpus` kind sends the report to the owner as a judgment issue ([merge.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/merge.md#L33)). The kinds come from a path list in the review script, [review:OWNER_PATHS](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/review#L45-L62), which classes every path under `.ok-planner/design/` as corpus, discover-design's `_discover/` notes included. The converge core's repoint of retired script paths skips only files that list classes as record or suite ([converge:caller_kind](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/converge#L1691)), so it rewrote a `_discover/` note and made it false. When sprint certification for [2026-10-05-second-intake-drain](.ok-planner/history/sprints/2026-10-05-second-intake-drain.md) saw that, the merge rejected the report because the list classed the folder the same way at the base, and triage then routed it as a question, reading a change to the list as a change to the corpus. Nothing in the ownership test says that where a corpus rule decides what kind a file is, a list that classes it otherwise is itself the site of a defect under [A8](.ok-planner/review/catalog/accept.md#L16), with its fix in project code. The owner, on reading it: "you were able to see the defect. and it's a clear defect. why do we need to be involved?"

The state of play. The instance is ruled: converge-repoints-observation-notes-and-migration-docs carries the owner's ruling that the `_discover/` notes are records converge leaves as written, and it awaits a sprint. This repository no longer shows the instance, since the owner moved its notes to `.ok-planner/history/discover/`. Triage already has the rule: [triage.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/triage-issues/prompts/triage.md#L37) routes `defect` where "the corpus or a stated rule decides the end state, and only the mechanism is open", and its doubt test asks whether a fixer must edit a file under `.ok-planner/design/`. The habit that stands is the merge reading a code list's classing as the rule.

The ruling decides how far the prompts change to stop that habit.

messages.text:
Every sprint work item changes the product: its code, configuration, documents, or design corpus. A work item that consists of using what the sprint builds is refused and reshaped into the feature, script, or seed asset that lets a user reach the outcome. The rule is stated in [concept:sprint](.ok-planner/design/concepts/sprint.md)'s Boundaries, in the planning session's drafting step, and in the work item template, and the code planner enforces it: a work item that changes no file cannot be built as drafted and goes back to the draft. The execution boilerplate states that execution and certification need no owner action and file no task for the owner to perform.

Rationale: this is option D with A's statements. The code planner already reads every work item against the code it touches and already sends back an item it cannot build, so an item that touches nothing fails a check that exists, before approval, with no new scope at sign-off. Option B leaves the rule with no check, which the project's Mechanical Checks rule forbids. Option C adds refusals downstream that could retire a real certification gap, and [concept:issue](.ok-planner/design/concepts/issue.md) already keeps tasks out of the intake. Option A catches the item one step earlier but widens a review built for corpus deltas. Flip case: if an operator-act item reaches approval because it also carries a small code change that passes the code planner, move the check to sign-off as in A, where the reviewer reads what each item's outcome is rather than whether it touches a file.

options.label: A
options.text: State the rule in the Draft phase, the Work items template, and [concept:sprint](.ok-planner/design/concepts/sprint.md); have the sign-off review check every work item against it; and state in the execution boilerplate that execution and certification need no owner action. Cost: sign-off gains a work-item scope it does not have today.

options.label: B
options.text: State the rule in the same places, with no check. Cost: no check fails on violation, against the project's Mechanical Checks rule.

options.label: C
options.text: Option A, and also have /converge's owner list and /triage-issues refuse an issue whose resolution is an act the owner performs on a running product. Cost: a real certification gap phrased as an owner act could be retired unread.

options.label: D
options.text: State the rule as in A, and make the code planner's existing kick-back test refuse a work item that changes no file in the tree, sending it back to be reshaped into the feature, script, or seed asset that lets a user reach the outcome. Cost: the item is caught only once code planning starts, after the deltas are reviewed.

problem:
Nothing in planning stops a sprint work item from being an act of using what the sprint builds, so execution spends a build task operating a stack, certification cannot see the result, and the run hands the owner a task. That breaks the promise in [story:plan-a-sprint](.ok-planner/design/stories/plan-a-sprint.md) that any executor can realize the sprint without re-deriving it, and the promise in [story:certify-completion](.ok-planner/design/stories/certify-completion.md) that the owner knows at the close whether what was approved was delivered.

A consumer project at ok-planner v25.3.0 hit this. Its sprint carried the features a 'test data in the lake' stage needed, and a twelfth item, 'the local stack seeded', whose outcome was data an operator makes on a developer stack by running those features. The owner approved it. Execution filed a build task that ran the stack, pushed scripts, and played back recorded captures. Certification then filed an issue asking the owner to confirm the seeded state by hand before the sprint closed. That owner ruled, in that project, that using a sprint's features is never part of a sprint, that execution needs no owner action during or after it, and that the intake never holds an operator task. This record carries no ruling of its own; the change lands in this repository, which owns the plan-sprint and converge skills.

The mechanism. The Work items template in [sprint-document.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-sprint/sprint-document.md#L35-L40) asks only for 'the implementation units that realize the deltas' and says each 'describes the outcome, not the method'; it never says the outcome is a change to the product. The sign-off review in [plan-sprint/SKILL.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-sprint/SKILL.md#L148-L150) checks the corpus deltas alone. The code planner can already kick back a work item that 'cannot be built as drafted' ([core.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-sprint/core.md#L274-L276)), but its tests name contradictions and missing prerequisites, not an item that changes no file. Execution's boilerplate says to 'work unsupervised to a defensible done' ([sprint-document.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-sprint/sprint-document.md#L170)). Certification judges the tree, the checks over the changed files, and a drive on a fresh stack of its own, so it cannot judge state left on a developer stack. Its owner list ([converge/SKILL.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/SKILL.md#L123)) files 'every other item that needs the owner's judgment', and nothing there refuses an operator task.

The state of play. The corpus defines a sprint's work items only as the items that realize its deltas ([concept:sprint](.ok-planner/design/concepts/sprint.md)), and no artifact says a work item must change the product. [concept:issue](.ok-planner/design/concepts/issue.md) already says the intake is a holding area, not a work tracker. The project rule that every written constraint needs a check that fails on violation ([`.claude/rules/plumbline-cheatsheet.md`](.claude/rules/plumbline-cheatsheet.md), Mechanical Checks) means a statement alone does not suffice. Each option below pairs with an amendment to [concept:sprint](.ok-planner/design/concepts/sprint.md)'s Boundaries stating the rule, since the rule adds a promise.

The ruling decides whether a sprint work item must change the product, and which step of planning refuses one that does not.

recommendation.text:
Every sprint work item changes the product: its code, configuration, documents, or design corpus. A work item that consists of using what the sprint builds is refused and reshaped into the feature, script, or seed asset that lets a user reach the outcome. The rule is stated in [concept:sprint](.ok-planner/design/concepts/sprint.md)'s Boundaries, in the planning session's drafting step, and in the work item template, and the code planner enforces it: a work item that changes no file cannot be built as drafted and goes back to the draft. The execution boilerplate states that execution and certification need no owner action and file no task for the owner to perform.

Rationale: this is option D with A's statements. The code planner already reads every work item against the code it touches and already sends back an item it cannot build, so an item that touches nothing fails a check that exists, before approval, with no new scope at sign-off. Option B leaves the rule with no check, which the project's Mechanical Checks rule forbids. Option C adds refusals downstream that could retire a real certification gap, and [concept:issue](.ok-planner/design/concepts/issue.md) already keeps tasks out of the intake. Option A catches the item one step earlier but widens a review built for corpus deltas. Flip case: if an operator-act item reaches approval because it also carries a small code change that passes the code planner, move the check to sign-off as in A, where the reviewer reads what each item's outcome is rather than whether it touches a file.

title: A sprint can carry a work item that only uses the product, which no unsupervised executor can build or certification can judge

messages.text:
Sprint certification drives every story, not only the stories the sprint adds or amends. A failure the sprint's change caused is fixed before the sprint closes. A failure in code the change did not reach goes to the intake by the existing scope test, where the next sprint pulls it in.

Rationale: option A is the only option that delivers the owner's rule that a later sprint never meets a legacy failure as a surprise, and it also catches what option C misses: a sprint that breaks a story it does not amend is caught inside its own certification, where the fix is in scope, instead of at the next planning session as legacy. Option C pays the same full drive per sprint but finds that regression only after the sprint has closed. Option B costs less but its reach ends where the annotations end. Option D leaves the gap the owner hit. The decision's own rationale already accepts that a drive pays to drive every story, so A extends a cost the project chose rather than adding a new kind. Flip case: if a full drive per certification costs more than the owner will pay, for a project with many stories or with drives widened by drive-pass-is-one-try, take C, which keeps one full drive per sprint at the planning session and keeps certification at its current cost.

options.label: A
options.text: Sprint certification drives every story. Cost: every certification pays a full drive run's cost, which the decision names as where a run spends its tokens.

options.label: B
options.text: Sprint certification drives the sprint's stories and every story whose citing code the change touched, found by the story annotations in the changed files. Cost: it misses a story whose code carries no annotation, and a story broken through code it calls but does not cite.

options.label: C
options.text: The planning session refuses to start until a full drive run has passed since the last sprint closed, and that run files each failure as a defect issue the sprint can pull in. Cost: a full drive run per sprint, and a new gate the decision and the planning skill must name.

options.label: D
options.text: The planning session reports at its start how many sprints have closed since the last full drive run and offers one, without refusing. Cost: the owner's cadence stays the only guard.

problem:
Sprint certification drives only the stories its sprint adds or amends, and nothing sets when a full drive of every story must run, so a story broken by earlier work can stay undriven across many sprints. [story:certify-completion](.ok-planner/design/stories/certify-completion.md) promises the owner a way to know at each close whether what was approved was delivered, so that 'done' means the same thing for every sprint; a sprint that closes with an older story failing, unknown to the owner, breaks that.

A consumer project at ok-planner v25.3.0 showed the gap. Its last full drive run drove 71 stories. Thirteen certifications followed, each driving only its own sprint's stories. The fourteenth amended 19 stories and met four failures in code that stood the same at its base: a device's record listing filtering --since and --until on the wrong field, a records page that failed whole with a 502 when another table was dropped mid-read, a mark stepper whose first Next did not move the chart, and two pages rounding one position accuracy two ways. No issue in the intake or its archive had named any of the four sites. The owner said that with every open issue pulled into each sprint, there should never be a surprise story failure from legacy code. The owner keeps the scope test that sends a defect outside the sprint to the intake.

The mechanism. [decision:drive-tries-each-story-as-a-user](.ok-planner/design/decisions/drive-tries-each-story-as-a-user.md) fixes the scope in its Choice: '/converge in drive mode gives every story its own driver once per run, and sprint certification does the same for the stories a sprint adds or amends.' Certification's drive step runs 'over those stories alone' ([converge/SKILL.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/SKILL.md#L102)). Its merge sends a real failure whose code stood the same at the base to the intake and lets the sprint close ([merge.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/merge.md#L48)). A full drive run happens only when the owner starts one. So a story no sprint touches is driven only on the owner's cadence, and a sprint's change that breaks a story the sprint does not amend is not driven at all at its close.

The state of play. The scope test works as the owner wants. What is missing is a step that drives every story often enough that a failure reaches the intake before a later sprint stumbles on it. Every option edits the decision's Choice. This issue rules together with drive-pass-is-one-try, which decides how much one drive covers, and merge-sorts-drive-failures-off-the-story.

The ruling decides which step drives the stories a sprint does not touch, and how often.

title: Sprint certification drives only the sprint's own stories, so a story broken earlier surfaces as a surprise in a later sprint

messages.text:
A drive covers every variant the story's own text names, and acts in the order a first-time user would, before it may pass a surface. Where a story says its benefit comes several ways, such as results narrowed by time and by field values, each named way gets driven and judged on its own, just as each surface is today. The driver reports each variant it drove, so the merge can see what a pass covers.

Rationale: option D bounds the drive by the story, which is the promise certification judges, so it widens the drive exactly as far as the owner's own words go and keeps the decision's rule that nothing about a drive is written down between runs. It catches both failures the owner met: the time narrowing the story named, and the first Next a new user presses on a freshly loaded page. Option A has no bound but the product's size, and leaves the merge judging a list's completeness with nothing to judge it against. Option B doubles the cost of every drive with no assurance the second driver differs. Option C keeps the harm. Flip case: if passes keep hiding failures on paths no story names, the stories are too thin for the product, and the fix is either to sharpen those stories or to take option A for the surfaces where that happens.

options.label: A
options.text: The driver lists, before it drives, every path to the benefit on each surface (each verb and flag, each page control, each order a user may act in), drives each, and reports the list; the merge treats a listed path left undriven as an incomplete drive. Cost: it grows with the product's flags and controls, and the merge must judge whether the list is complete.

options.label: B
options.text: Each story gets two independent drivers, and passes only where both pass. Cost: every drive costs twice as much, and both drivers may take the same path.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep one path per surface. Cost: a pass can still hide a failing path.

options.label: D
options.text: The driver drives every variant the story's own text names, such as each way a story says its results can be narrowed, and acts in the order a first-time user would, then reports each variant it drove. Cost: a path the story's text does not name stays untried.

problem:
A driver closes a story achieved as soon as one path on a surface delivers the benefit, so the story's other paths go untried and a pass says only that one path worked. Sprint certification reads that pass as the story working, which breaks [story:certify-completion](.ok-planner/design/stories/certify-completion.md)'s promise that the owner knows at each close whether what was approved was delivered.

A consumer project at ok-planner v25.3.0 met this twice. A certification drove a story about stepping through marks on a waveform and closed it achieved. Two days later another certification's driver pressed Next first on a freshly loaded page: the label advanced to '1 of 6' and the chart did not move, in code that had not changed between the two drives. Earlier, a certification drove a story promising to list the records a table or a device holds 'narrowed by time and by the values of their fields', and closed it achieved. The device listing's --since and --until filtered on a different field than its help named, and a later driver that narrowed a device listing by time got an empty page. The first driver never narrowed a device listing by time.

The mechanism. The drive prompt has the driver try each surface a story is offered through and judge each on its own ([drive.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/drive.md#L23)), then 'stop at the first' outcome, where achieved means 'you got the benefit the so-that clause names' ([drive.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/drive.md#L41-L43)). The only other path it asks for is a refusal the story promises ([drive.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/drive.md#L48)). So a flag the driver did not pass, a control it did not press first, or an order of actions it did not take stays untried.

The state of play. [decision:drive-tries-each-story-as-a-user](.ok-planner/design/decisions/drive-tries-each-story-as-a-user.md) asks the driver to get the benefit 'on every surface the story is offered through', never on every path within a surface, and keeps nothing about a drive written down between runs. Widening a drive widens what that decision commits a drive to. This issue rules together with sprint-certification-drives-only-sprint-stories, which decides how many stories a certification drives, so the two costs multiply, and with merge-sorts-drive-failures-off-the-story.

The ruling decides how much of a story one drive must cover before it may pass.

title: A driver stops at the first path that delivers a story, so a pass can hide a path the story names that fails

messages.text: Rewrite the drive's-failures section of converge's merge prompt. It now sorts a stuck story whose user lacked a page, a verb, or a flow as not-owed, sorts as not-owed any failure the corpus does not decide, and names only [A3](.ok-planner/review/catalog/accept.md#L11) as the entry. After the change it says: a failure is a defect wherever the story's text, or a decision it cites, names what the driver could not get, a missing flow included, and a page or message that tells the user something false is a defect whatever a work item says; not-owed applies only where the driver sought something beyond the story's text and its decisions; a sprint work item never decides what a story owes, and in sprint mode a work item that contradicts a story is a commitment contradicted ([C4](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_sprint/shared.md#L277)); and A3 and [A8](.ok-planner/review/catalog/accept.md#L16) cover every story failure, so no line of what the accept list leaves standing clears one. The stuck rule's message clause stays as one way a stuck story is a defect, not the only way. The backlog scope test stays. The rule that forces it: [decision:drive-tries-each-story-as-a-user](.ok-planner/design/decisions/drive-tries-each-story-as-a-user.md) sorts each failure by what the story or a decision owes, and [decision:accept-list-decides-defects](.ok-planner/design/decisions/accept-list-decides-defects.md) has the merge sort drive failures against the list, whose A3 names every failure the drive records. Nothing was applied.

options.label: A
options.text: State in the merge prompt that a drive failure is a defect wherever the product does not deliver what the story's text names, a missing flow and a page or message that tells the user something false included; that not-owed applies only where the driver sought something beyond the story's text and its decisions; that a sprint work item never decides what a story owes; and that A3 and A8 cover a story failure, so no line of what the list leaves standing clears it. Cost: a merge agent must read the story's benefit closely on every stuck failure.

options.label: B
options.text: Option A, and every stuck or not-owed sort quotes the story to show its text does not name what the driver sought; a sort without the quote is refiled. Cost: one more refile round for each bad sort.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep the prompt as it stands and let the owner rule each not-owed question at /plan-sprint. Cost: the owner's attention on each, and sprints close with failing stories meanwhile.

problem:
Converge's merge prompt lets a merge agent clear a drive failure whose story the product does not meet, so a sprint can close with a story failing and no defect on the list. That breaks [decision:drive-tries-each-story-as-a-user](.ok-planner/design/decisions/drive-tries-each-story-as-a-user.md), which says a merge agent sorts each failure "as a defect the story or a decision owes, as something the corpus does not promise, or as a failure of the environment": the test is what the story owes.

The mechanism. In drive mode, and in sprint certification's drive, one driver per story tries to get the story's benefit through the running product and reports each failure as `failed`, `stuck`, or `blocked`. A merge agent then sorts each failure under [merge.md, "The drive's failures"](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/merge.md#L40-L50). Three lines there let it sort by something other than the story:

1. The stuck rule sorts by the failure's kind. [merge.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/merge.md#L44) says "A stuck story with no such message (the user needed a page, a verb, or a flow the product does not offer) is not a defect for this run: sort it `not-owed`". Where the story's benefit is that very flow, the missing flow is the story failing, and the same bullet's own test (the story says the product owes it) calls it a defect. In the filed case, a story promised going "from a device named on a chart to what that unit is ... without writing a query"; the driver found no link and no search that matched, and the merge sorted it not-owed because the flow does not exist.
2. The undecided rule lets a lesser source decide. [merge.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/merge.md#L50) sorts a failure not-owed "Where the corpus does not decide whether the product owes what the driver tried to get", and nothing tells the merge that a sprint work item is neither the story nor a decision. In the filed case, a page headed a section with a time and wrote "No reference yet" for a pair whose reference had been in force half an hour earlier. The merge sorted it not-owed because a work item said a card with no id in the window shows that text. A page that tells the user something false fails the story whatever a work item says; in sprint mode the work item's wording contradicting the story is [C4](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_sprint/shared.md#L277), a commitment contradicted.
3. Nothing says which entry covers a story failure. [The converge skill](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/SKILL.md#L22) opens with "The accept list decides what is a defect", and step 2 of report judging ([merge.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/merge.md#L20)) applies the list to the harm. The drive section names only "entry A3 unless another entry fits better". In the filed case, a story promised the operator sees "how accurate the fix is"; the map read ±5 m and the device page 4 m for a reported 4.5 m, and the merge rejected it as a harm "the accept list leaves ... standing".

The state of play. The accept list already covers every one of these: [A3](.ok-planner/review/catalog/accept.md#L11) names "every failure the drive records" among its sites, and [A8](.ok-planner/review/catalog/accept.md#L16) counts a breach of "a commitment of a live artifact under .ok-planner/design/". [decision:accept-list-decides-defects](.ok-planner/design/decisions/accept-list-decides-defects.md) says "the merge sorts those failures against the list", so the fix is not to take the drive off the list but to say that the list covers a story failure. The filed option A's clause "the accept list does not clear a drive failure" contradicts that decision as worded; the options below reword it. The owner keeps the scope test that sends a defect outside a sprint to the backlog. The drivers tested the promised behavior; the merge cleared the failures.

The ruling decides how the merge prompt states the drive's defect test.

title: The merge sorts a story failure as not owed when the story names what the driver could not get

messages.text:
An issue the owner has never opened counts as new analysis. The intake records when the owner first opens each issue, from the command line or the dashboard, and the unread mark covers an issue never opened as well as one with unread agent messages. Every issue already in the intake counts as opened when the record field arrives, so the owner does not see the whole intake turn new at once. The decision on agent revisions says that filing reaches the owner, though a first routing stays silent. The dashboard's unread tab lists verified defect issues as it lists every other kind.

Rationale: option A gives the story's 'since I last read them' its plain meaning, since an issue the owner has never opened has never been read, and it keeps the one signal on the owner's own act, the same act that marks agent messages read. Option B reaches the same mark through the existing count, but it puts a message into every issue that carries no analysis, against the decision's own reason for keeping a first routing silent: a signal that inflates the count. Option C leaves verified defect issues with no signal at all. Option D cannot follow the owner across browsers or the command line. Flip case: if the owner wants no change to the record's schema, B is the smaller change and delivers the same mark.

options.label: A
options.text: Record when the owner first opens each issue, from the command line or the dashboard, and mark an issue never opened as new; existing issues count as opened when the field arrives, and [agent-revisions-reach-the-owner](.ok-planner/design/decisions/agent-revisions-reach-the-owner.md), or a new decision, says filing counts as new analysis. Cost: a new record field and a one-time migration.

options.label: B
options.text: Have filing write one unread 'filed' message for every issue an agent files, never for one the owner files, so the existing unread count carries it. Cost: no schema change, but every issue carries one message that says nothing beyond its own fields.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep the behavior, and amend the decision's rationale to name 'needs ruling' as the signal for a judgment issue and the planning session's defect list as the signal for a defect issue. Cost: the owner's harm stands.

options.label: D

problem:
The intake's unread count counts only agent messages, and a newly filed issue has none, so the dashboard marks no new issue as unread. [story:see-new-analysis](.ok-planner/design/stories/see-new-analysis.md) promises the owner a way to see which issues have new answers or revisions since the owner last read them, and an issue the owner has never opened is the case the mark misses.

A project owner opened the dashboard on an intake of 10 issues, all filed in one run the day before, and expected each to show as unread. None did. Four were verified defect issues and six needed a ruling.

The mechanism. [issues:unread](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/issues#L473-L474) counts agent messages whose read time is unset. A filed record starts with no messages ([issues:defaults](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/issues#L611-L613)), because an issue's first analysis lives in its problem, options, and recommendation fields. Triage's first routing of an issue writes no message either ([issues](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/issues#L708)). The dashboard's [isUnread](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/browser/src/lib/api.js#L79) tests that count, and the issue list shows its 'N new' tag only where that test holds ([IssueList.svelte](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/browser/src/views/IssueList.svelte#L73)). No field records whether the owner has ever opened an issue; marking an issue read marks its agent messages and nothing else. The dashboard's 'unread' tab also leaves verified issues out ([api.js](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/browser/src/lib/api.js#L87)), so a defect issue never lists there even when it holds unread messages.

The state of play. The corpus chose this for routing. [decision:agent-revisions-reach-the-owner](.ok-planner/design/decisions/agent-revisions-reach-the-owner.md) says a first routing stays silent, because a first routing already shows the issue as needing a ruling. That rationale covers routing, not filing. It also fails twice: 'needs ruling' says an issue waits on the owner, not that the owner has never seen it, and a verified defect issue never needs a ruling, so a new one carries no signal at all. [decision:closed-answers-count-as-new](.ok-planner/design/decisions/closed-answers-count-as-new.md) covers answers on closed issues only.

The ruling decides whether an issue the owner has never opened counts as new analysis, and how the intake records it.

recommendation.text:
An issue the owner has never opened counts as new analysis. The intake records when the owner first opens each issue, from the command line or the dashboard, and the unread mark covers an issue never opened as well as one with unread agent messages. The decision on agent revisions says that filing reaches the owner, though a first routing stays silent. The dashboard's unread tab lists verified defect issues as it lists every other kind.

problem:

Its final report ([SKILL.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/discover-design/SKILL.md#L62)) and its re-run section offer no step that moves them. Some readers already skip them: the artifact rules call them "point-in-time and exempt" ([artifact-definitions.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_shared/artifact-definitions.md#L339)), and the compliance reviewer flags "nothing under `_discover/`" ([design-doc-compliance-reviewer.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_shared/design-doc-compliance-reviewer.md#L228)). problem:
Site: [dashboard:Start the service](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/dashboard/SKILL.md#L22) and [dashboard:Report](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/dashboard/SKILL.md#L38), steps 2 and 3 of the /dashboard skill.

Entry: [A3](.ok-planner/review/catalog/accept.md#L11). An action a user takes through the public surface (the /dashboard verb) leaves the product in a state where later use fails: a stall.

Trigger: the owner runs /dashboard, then hands a sprint to the native goal mechanism in the same session (`/goal <path-to-sprint>`), as [ok-planner-CLAUDE.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/ok-planner-CLAUDE.md#L554-L555) invites: "so a sprint can be handed to the native goal mechanism (`/goal <path-to-sprint>`)".

Harm: Claude Code defers a goal's check while any background task of the session runs. The skill starts a service that never exits on its own as such a task, and forbids the session to stop it, so the goal's check is deferred again and again and the goal never completes, however finished the sprint is.

Evidence: [SKILL.md:22](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/dashboard/SKILL.md#L22) reads "run `python3 .ok-planner/bin/dashboard --open` with the Bash tool's `run_in_background` set", and [SKILL.md:38](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/dashboard/SKILL.md#L38) reads "The service keeps running while the owner works. Do not stop it on your own initiative." In session 52cf998e, at 2026-10-06T10:26 the harness wrote "evaluation has been deferred for 30 min because background work is still running", listing a dashboard service started the same way and a Vite dev server; at 11:26 the same at 60 min. Once the session stopped both, the goal check ran and passed at once.

[decision:dashboard-started-by-skill](.ok-planner/design/decisions/dashboard-started-by-skill.md) reads "A vendored `/dashboard` skill starts the dashboard's service in the background of the owner's session". A service the skill starts as a detached process, its serving line read from a file, still runs in the background of the owner's session and still stops on `kill <pid>`, so the fix leaves the decision as it stands.

recommendation.text: Fix [dashboard:Start the service](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/dashboard/SKILL.md#L22) so a running dashboard no longer holds a goal's check open.

title: A dashboard started by /dashboard keeps a /goal on a sprint from ever being checked

messages.text:
Option B. A run's artifacts end with the run: the tag's life is mint, build, verify, remove. The run's stack stop removes everything the run built under its tag, whether the run passed or failed, and the periodic cleanup that frees stale port leases also removes the artifacts of every run tag that holds no lease and has no containers left. The rules layer states this as part of the suite's own per-run rule, beside the port registry, and the stop role in the project's facts names removal as part of its job. Land it in the same sprint as the port registry ruling, since both rewrite the same rule.

Rationale: the owner ruled that the port registry is one of the suite's own opinionated rules, with leases ending when the run's stack goes down and a periodic cleanup for runs that never got there. Artifacts have the same life as leases, so they end at the same two points, and the registry's leases supply the live-or-dead test the cleanup needs. Option A alone leaves a crashed run's images on disk forever, which is the harm this issue names. Option C adds a role every project must fill and still misses the audit's experiment runs, where B's cleanup reaches every run tag whatever started it. Option D leaves the default broken, against [decision:per-run-artifact-tag](.ok-planner/design/decisions/per-run-artifact-tag.md)'s own claim that a tag never outlives its run. A failed run's evidence lives in its service logs and its recorded output, and a rerun rebuilds under a fresh tag, so keeping a failed run's images buys little. The flip case: if owners debug failed runs by entering their images, the stack stop should keep a failed run's artifacts and leave them to the periodic cleanup.

options.label: A
options.text: **Remove at stack-stop.** Amend [decision:per-run-artifact-tag](.ok-planner/design/decisions/per-run-artifact-tag.md) so the tag's life ends with removing what the run built under it, and have the rules layer and the `stack-stop` role tell the project's stop command to remove the run's artifacts (for a compose stack, its images and volumes). Cost: a run that crashes before its stack stops still leaks.

options.label: B
options.text: **Remove at stack-stop, and in the periodic cleanup.** Option A, plus the periodic cleanup the port registry ruling adds, widened to remove the artifacts of every `run-` tag that holds no lease and has no containers left. Cost: the cleanup must know the project's artifact kinds, so beyond container images it relies on the project's own stop command to name what to remove.

options.label: C
options.text: **A role of its own.** Add a drive role, such as `artifact-remove`, that the converge skill runs after `stack-stop` in the drive, the confirm step, and sprint certification. Cost: one more role every project must fill, and the audit's experiment runs need the same step, which no role reaches today.

options.label: D
options.text: **Leave it to the project.** Keep the corpus as it stands, with removal the project's own wiring under the run-tag concept's Boundaries, and add one sentence to the rules layer saying so. Cost: the leak stays open by default in every project that follows the rule.

problem:
The suite's rule for verification runs says when a run's tag is born and how it is used, and says nothing about when what the run built goes away. Every verification run mints a fresh tag and builds every artifact it verifies under that tag, as [decision:per-run-artifact-tag](.ok-planner/design/decisions/per-run-artifact-tag.md) requires. No step of that rule, of the drive's stack roles, or of any suite tool removes those artifacts once the run ends.

## How it happens

The rules layer, in its section on per-run artifacts and verification stacks ([ok-planner-cheatsheet.md:354-364](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/ok-planner-cheatsheet.md#L354-L364)), reads: "Every verification run mints one fresh tag, builds every artifact it verifies under that tag", and "never any tag that outlives the run, in a verification path". The tag must not outlive the run in a verification path, yet nothing makes the artifact it names end with the run.

The review loop runs the project's stack through roles the project fills in its facts file ([review/seed/project.md:27](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/review/seed/project.md#L27)): `stack-start`, `stack-stop`, `instance-create`, `instance-destroy`, `resource-start`, `resource-stop`, `service-log`, and `sign-in`. None is asked to remove the run's images. The converge skill's stop steps ([converge SKILL.md:79](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/SKILL.md#L79), and again in the confirm step at [line 114](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/SKILL.md#L114)) run only `stack-stop`, `instance-destroy`, and `resource-stop`. A grep of `plugins/` for `rmi`, `image rm`, `image prune`, and `--rmi` finds nothing.

The tag is unique to the run, so no later build reuses or replaces an earlier run's images. Each `/converge` drive, sprint certification, and audit experiment run in a project whose verification path builds container images adds a full set. The owner sees nothing until a build fails for lack of disk space, then prunes by hand. This project has no stack of its own, so the harm falls on consumer projects.

## What the corpus says

[decision:per-run-artifact-tag](.ok-planner/design/decisions/per-run-artifact-tag.md) gives the tag's life as mint, build, and verify. The concept [run-tag](.ok-planner/design/concepts/run-tag.md), under Boundaries, says "wiring it into builds, stacks, and harnesses is deliberately the project's own change, guided by the rules layer". So the corpus leaves open whether removal is the suite's rule or the project's own wiring, and a fixer cannot choose without changing the decision or the concept. The accept list covers the harm only weakly: entry [A5](.ok-planner/review/catalog/accept.md#L13), ongoing work that wears down while the system looks healthy, names repeating work and acquires in a long-running process, and a verification run is short-lived. That is why this is a question and not a defect.

## The ruled sibling

The owner's ruling on [port-block-reads-back-a-stale-record](.ok-planner/issues.jsonl) replaces the port read-back with a project-local port registry. It ends a run's leases when the run's stack goes down, and adds a periodic cleanup that frees each lease whose port nothing holds and whose compose project has no containers left. It also has the suite's per-run section rewritten as one of the suite's own rules. Those are the two points where removing a run's artifacts would also run, and the registry's leases tell a live run's tag from a dead one's.

The ruling decides whether a run's artifacts end with the run as a suite rule, and if so, where removal runs: at the stack's stop, in a periodic cleanup for runs that never reached the stop, or in a role of its own.

problem:
Site: [converge/prompts/sprint-pass.md:Your reading](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/sprint-pass.md#L17).

Entry: A3, an end user can break the product. `/converge sprint` is an action a user takes through the public surface.

Trigger: `/converge sprint` reissues a pass task to a fresh agent, and the sprint's change touches a file in a folder `.ok-planner/config.json` declares under `folders`, or in a folder the sprint lists under '## Paths outside the project root'.

Harm: the action gives a wrong result. `.ok-planner/bin/review changed` lists such a file as a path starting `../`, and `git diff --relative` limits git's output to the current directory, so the pass reads an empty diff and reviews no change in that file. This breaks [decision:project-declares-its-folders](.ok-planner/design/decisions/project-declares-its-folders.md): 'Every tool that lists or scopes the project's code reads that list: the review tool in every /converge mode'.

Evidence: [sprint-pass.md#L17](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/sprint-pass.md#L17) reads 'each file's diff from `git diff --relative [BASE] -- <path>`'. The sibling [sprint-review.md#L20](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/sprint-review.md#L20) reads the same list 'as paths starting `../`' and reads 'each file's diff with `git diff [BASE] -- <path>`', with no `--relative`. From a scratch repository's project root `app/`, `git diff --relative HEAD -- ../shared/util.py` printed nothing (exit 0), and `git diff HEAD -- ../shared/util.py` printed the change.

A merge agent confirmed it in run converge-2026-10-14T050729 (drive failure i10).

recommendation.text: Fix [converge/prompts/sprint-pass.md:Your reading](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/sprint-pass.md#L17) so a reissued pass no longer reviews no change in a file under a declared folder.

title: A reissued sprint pass reads an empty diff for every file in a declared folder

messages.text:
What we want here is a very simple system: one tool or verb family that manages a stack's whole lifecycle, with whatever local state or registry it needs, plus the practices projects must follow to make that tool work reliably.

A run that needs a stack provisions it with one verb and retires it with another. Provision mints the run tag, leases the ports, and writes one registry entry for the run. Every artifact the stack builds is recorded against that entry: provision hands the stack a docker label with the run tag, and the stack applies it to each image, volume, and network. Retire stops the stack, removes every artifact the entry records, releases the lease, and deletes the entry. Cleanup retires each stale entry the registry lists. It never scans docker for names, so it never touches another project's artifacts. Drives, tests, and the audit's experiments all provision their stacks this way.

Site: [scripts/ports:cleanup](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/ports#L450-L473), with [remove_artifacts](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/ports#L442-L447).

Entry: A5, ongoing work stops or wears down while the system still looks healthy: the periodic cleanup stops making progress, and one bad item blocks it forever. A8 also holds: [plumbline-coding.md](.claude/rules/plumbline-coding.md#L43), rule 4 step 2, says 'A cleanup loop attempts every item and raises the first failure after the loop, never abandons the rest on the first raise', and that rule decides the fix.

Trigger: `docker image rm` refuses an image for a reason no container causes, such as an image with dependent child images, or an image a container started between the in-use check and the removal uses.

Harm: the refusal raises DockerFailed out of the loop over the dead run tags, sorted, so every tag after it stays uncleaned. A refusal that persists, such as dependent child images, stops the cleanup at the same tag on every later run. The fix for defect i44 skips a tag whose artifacts a container uses; it does not cover these refusals.

messages.text:
The back-edge serves every artifact kind: the phase 2 reviewer may request a second read for a thin concept, story, or decision, names the kind and slug in each request, and may authorize a new artifact of any kind, matching what the extractor already expects. The story stays as it stands, since its promise holds and the back-edge's scope is the skill's mechanism.

Rationale: The story's purpose is that the owner's attention goes to genuine ambiguities, and the reviewer's own test for a request, that the fix is reading more code rather than making a design decision, holds for a story or a decision as much as for a concept. Under A, each such gap becomes an issue the owner must read, which spends the attention the story protects. B also aligns the reviewer with the extractor, which is already written for all three kinds, so the skill speaks one request shape. The back-edge still runs at most once per invocation, which bounds its larger cost. Flip case: if back-edge runs show second reads of stories and decisions coming back unchanged, the extra cost buys nothing, and A is the better call.

options.label: A
options.text: Concepts alone: the extractor's story and decision branches are cut, and its promotion field becomes 'Promote new concept'. Cost: a thin story or decision gets no second read, only an issue for the owner.

options.label: B
options.text: Every kind: the reviewer names the kind and slug in each request and may authorize a new artifact of any kind, and its inclusion test covers stories and decisions. Cost: a larger back-edge, and a reviewer prompt that judges thinness for three kinds.

problem:

A run that needs a stack provisions it with one verb and retires it with another. Provision mints the run tag, leases the ports, and writes one registry entry for the run. options.label: A
options.text: Exact match: the decision run-artifacts-removed-with-the-run says a run's image carries the run tag as its whole tag or as its repository's prefix, and the rules layer tells the owner to tag images with the run tag alone. Cost: a suffixed build still fills the disk until someone removes it by hand, and the owner learns the rule only from the rules text.

options.label: B
options.text: Prefix match: the decision run-artifacts-removed-with-the-run says an image whose tag begins with the run tag followed by `-` or `_` is the run's, the boundary the repository match already uses, and the cleanup removes it under the same lease, container, and one-hour checks. Cost: one project's cleanup also deletes other projects' suffixed run images once those checks pass.

options.label: C
options.text: Exact match with a warning: the cleanup keeps the exact match, prints a line naming each image whose tag carries a run tag with a suffix, and leaves the image in place; the decision run-artifacts-removed-with-the-run says suffixed tags stay. Cost: the disk still fills until someone acts on the line.

problem:
ok-planner's port cleanup removes a crashed run's image only where the image's tag is exactly the run tag, so an image tagged with the run tag plus a suffix, such as `run-62dc11c74373-amd64`, stays on disk. That breaks the promise of [story:verification-leaves-no-artifacts-behind](.ok-planner/design/stories/verification-leaves-no-artifacts-behind.md) that each verification run's artifacts are removed once the run is over.

The cleanup lists every image docker knows, across every project on the machine. [scripts/ports:run_artifacts](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/ports#L411) assigns an image to a run tag in two ways: its tag matches `run-<12 hex>` exactly ([scripts/ports:RUN_TAG](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/ports#L75)), or its repository name begins with the run tag followed by `-` or `_` ([scripts/ports:COMPOSE_IMAGE](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/ports#L97)). A tag with a suffix matches neither, so the cleanup never sees the image. Its `removed:` line counts only the images it found, so the owner gets no word of the one left behind. Evidence: the cleanup printed 'removed: run-62dc11c74373 (1 image(s), 0 volume(s), 0 network(s))', and `docker image ls` then still listed 'vlnab-arch:run-62dc11c74373-amd64'. A multi-architecture build tags this way by habit: the driver's machine held 28 such images of another project, such as 'gridiq-allinone:run-d61aae7a593d-amd64' at 6.24GB.

The corpus does not settle which tags carry the run tag. [decision:run-artifacts-removed-with-the-run](.ok-planner/design/decisions/run-artifacts-removed-with-the-run.md) says the cleanup removes the images 'of every run tag that holds no lease', has no containers left, and has no artifact made in the last hour. [decision:per-run-artifact-tag](.ok-planner/design/decisions/per-run-artifact-tag.md) and [concept:run-tag](.ok-planner/design/concepts/run-tag.md) say a run builds every artifact it verifies under its tag, which reads as the tag itself, and neither forbids a suffix. The help text ([scripts/ports](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/ports#L60-L63)) says 'each image tagged with the run tag'. Because the cleanup reaches every project's images, the match also decides what one project's cleanup deletes for every other project. The decision already accepts that reach for exact tags, guarded by the lease, container, and one-hour checks.

The ruling decides which image tags count as a run's.

recommendation.text:
Count an image as a run's where its tag begins with the run tag followed by `-` or `_`, as well as where its tag is the run tag exactly, and remove it under the same lease, container, and one-hour checks the cleanup applies today. The decision on removing a run's artifacts says so, and the cleanup's help text names the suffixed form.

Rationale: The story promises that verification never fills the disk, and an architecture suffix is an ordinary way to tag a build, so the exact match (A) and the warning line (C) both leave the harm in place and hand the owner a manual step. The prefix match (B) puts the image tag on the same footing as the repository name, which the cleanup already matches with the same boundary. Its reach into other projects is the reach the decision already accepts for exact tags: twelve random hex digits after `run-` collide with no name a run did not mint, and the lease, container, and one-hour checks guard a live run the same way. Flip case: if an owner reports that the cleanup removed a suffixed image another project still needed, the cross-project reach outweighs the disk, and A with C's warning line becomes the better call.

It never scans docker for names, so it never touches another project's artifacts. Drives, tests, and the audit's experiments all provision their stacks this way.

Again seems like a clear defect. At the end of the sprint, the sprint is meant to be complete. "Should the corpus have been updated per the sprint" is not a thing that would ever need owner judgment.

options.label: A
options.text: Certification lands it: the decisions final-form-deltas and runs-fix-what-the-project-owns say that copying an approved delta of the run's own sprint into place verbatim is applying that sprint's deltas, and the ownership test lets certification's fixer make that one corpus write. Cost: a review run now writes the corpus, under a narrow exception the converge skill and merge prompt must carry.

options.label: C
options.text: Execution lands it: certification hands an unlanded delta back to sprint execution, which files a build task to land it before certification returns. Cost: certification no longer ends on its own terms, and the converge skill gains a step that reopens execution.

problem:
When a sprint's approved corpus delta did not land, sprint certification finds the gap but may not close it, so item 1 of the completion contract stays unmet and no run can reach the sprint's goal. That breaks [story:certify-completion](.ok-planner/design/stories/certify-completion.md), which promises that 'done' means the same thing for every sprint.

Sprint certification (`/converge sprint`) runs after every build task closes. Its alignment pass compares each delta with its artifact byte for byte and reports a mismatch under accept-list entry [C3](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_sprint/shared.md#L276) ([converge/prompts/sprint-pass.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/sprint-pass.md#L25)). The merge step then applies the ownership test to the file the fix lies in, 'even where the sprint's change edited the file or a delta names the artifact' ([converge/SKILL.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/SKILL.md#L103)): a fix in the corpus sets the item to judgment, with no fix round ([converge/prompts/merge.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/merge.md#L34)), and the owner list files it in the intake. The contract's item 1 reads 'Every corpus matches every delta above, applied verbatim' ([plan-sprint/sprint-document.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-sprint/sprint-document.md#L244)), and the goal rule exempts only 'A stuck defect listed in the return' ([plan-sprint/sprint-document.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-sprint/sprint-document.md#L258-L263)). A judgment item is not a stuck defect, so a goal checker either loops on a sprint no agent of the run may finish, or passes over item 1. Evidence: `review owner` in a scratch project printed 'corpus	.ok-planner/design/stories/subtract-numbers.md' for the sprint's own delta.

Four artifacts bear on it. [decision:final-form-deltas](.ok-planner/design/decisions/final-form-deltas.md) makes applying an approved sprint's deltas the only act that changes what the corpus commits to, and says no review run edits the corpus. [decision:runs-fix-what-the-project-owns](.ok-planner/design/decisions/runs-fix-what-the-project-owns.md) leaves the corpus alone and sends a corpus fix to the intake as a judgment issue. [decision:sprint-goal-read-from-the-repository](.ok-planner/design/decisions/sprint-goal-read-from-the-repository.md) holds the goal met when the contract's items verify, with a stuck defect as the one exemption. [concept:corpus-delta](.ok-planner/design/concepts/corpus-delta.md) gives certification the job of verifying that deltas landed, not of landing them. A delta a builder departed from on purpose reaches certification with a recorded build divergence, which the alignment pass already judges; the gap is the delta that simply did not land. The defect issue sprint-contract-stuck-check-two-verdicts rewrites the same goal rule's verdict on a stuck check, so this ruling lands before its fix or with it.

The ruling decides who lands an approved delta that execution missed, or whether the goal may close without it.

recommendation.text:
Sprint certification lands an approved delta of its own sprint that did not land and that no recorded build divergence explains: its fixer copies the delta's body into place verbatim, and its verifier checks the artifact byte for byte against the delta. The decisions on final-form deltas and on what a run fixes name this one write as applying the sprint's deltas, and every other corpus fix still goes to the intake.

Rationale: The owner signed off on the delta's exact text, so copying it into place changes nothing the owner has not approved, and the contract's item 1 keeps its force. Option B lets 'done' cover an approved change that never landed, against the story's promise. Option C keeps the line that no review run writes the corpus, but it reopens execution from inside certification for a step that needs no judgment and that certification's byte-for-byte check already verifies. The precedent in final-form-deltas is that the delta's exact text gives the sign-off its weight, not the agent that applies it. Flip case: if a delta that failed to land usually turns out to be a wrong delta, so that a builder should look before anyone copies it, C is the better call, since it keeps landing with execution and lets the builder record a fork.

ruling.text: Again seems like a clear defect. At the end of the sprint, the sprint is meant to be complete. "Should the corpus have been updated per the sprint" is not a thing that would ever need owner judgment.

title: Sprint certification finds its own sprint's unlanded delta and may not land it, so the goal never closes
