after.text:
Retire the issue: the ruling on stack-lifecycle-delegates-to-project-tooling removes the `stack` key from `.ok-planner/config.json`, so `stack.tag_variable` no longer exists and cannot collide with a declared port name. The sprint that carries that ruling removes the collision defect with the key, in [plumbline:stackDefects](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/plumbline#L297-L324) and [stack:stack_defects](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/stack#L288-L321), and true-up's config offer then names no key for it.

Rationale: the question of which name yields exists only while the stack tool sets a project-named variable to the run tag. Once the `stack` key retires, `ports` stays only as a setting the port registry reads, and no other config name competes with a port name.

before.text:
Keep the collision a stack defect: the owner repairs it by choosing another run-tag variable, and true-up's config offer refuses a port rename for it. Record in the corpus, beside the rule that binds host ports to declared port names, that the run-tag variable may not be a declared port name and that the variable is what yields.

Rationale: the config offer edits only the project's configuration, and the run-tag variable and the start command that reads it both live in one key there, so the offer can make the whole repair without touching a file the owner wrote elsewhere. A port rename (B) leaves every compose file and command that reads the port on the old name, which the compose port check then flags, so the offer would hand the owner the work the true-up story says an upgrade never costs. Accepting both keys (C) adds a special case to a rule that now has none, for a repair whose cheaper side is known. The flip case: if projects' compose files commonly read the run-tag variable too, such as for image tags, a variable rename reaches as many files as a port rename, and only the owner knows which is cheaper, so both keys (C) earns its special case.

messages.text: Recommendation now explains the retirement the ruling chose.

options.label: A
options.text: The collision is a stack defect (the code now): the corpus says the owner repairs it by choosing another run-tag variable, and true-up's config offer refuses a port rename. Cost: an owner who would rather rename the port edits the config by hand.

options.label: B
options.text: The collision is a ports defect: the defect text opens with `ports` again, the owner repairs it by renaming the port, and the offer refuses a run-tag variable change. Cost: the rename reaches every compose file and command that reads the port variable, which the offer cannot edit.

options.label: C
options.text: The collision belongs to both keys: true-up's config offer accepts a draft that changes either the run-tag variable or the port name. Cost: the one defect whose offer names two keys, a special case beside the rule that a defect's first word names its key.

problem:
When `.ok-planner/config.json` declares a port name that is also `stack.tag_variable`, the variable the stack tool sets to the run tag, true-up's config offer accepts only a draft that changes the `stack` key and refuses a draft that renames the port. No corpus artifact says which of the two names the owner repairs, and [story:true-up-project-estate](.ok-planner/design/stories/true-up-project-estate.md) owes the owner that upgrading the suite never costs them work they wrote.

The mechanism: `plumbline config-check` and `stack up` print the same defect, 'stack.tag_variable "<NAME>" is also a name ports declares, and the stack tool sets it to the run tag', from [plumbline:stackDefects](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/plumbline#L297-L324) and [stack:stack_defects](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/stack#L288-L321). True-up's [true-up:config_named_keys](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up#L2778-L2779) names each config key whose name opens a defect's text, and [true-up:changed_keys](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up#L2782-L2793) refuses a draft that changes any key not named, as [`admin/ADMINISTRATION.md`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md#L122) says of the `config` offer. So the first word of the defect text alone picks the key the owner may change: the text opens with `stack`, and a port rename is refused as 'ports (changed)'. The offer edits `.ok-planner/config.json` alone. The `stack` key holds the start command that reads the run-tag variable, so a draft can rename the variable and the start command's use of it in one key. A port name is read by the project's compose files and commands, which the offer does not touch, so a port rename inside the config alone leaves them reading the old name.

The state of play: before sprint certification of `2026-10-14-stack-lifecycle` (run converge-2026-10-15T011914), the text opened with 'ports', so the offer accepted only a port rename. The run's defect i16 re-worded it to open with `stack` and recorded the choice as question call i29, reasoning that a port rename reaches every compose file and command that reads the port variable, while the start command reads the run-tag variable. [decision:stack-ports-checked-as-a-suite-rule](.ok-planner/design/decisions/stack-ports-checked-as-a-suite-rule.md) binds each published host port to a declared port name and says nothing of the run-tag variable.

The ruling decides which name true-up's config offer lets the owner change when the two collide.

The sprint that carries that ruling removes the collision defect with the key, in [plumbline:stackDefects](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/plumbline#L297-L324) and [stack:stack_defects](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/stack#L288-L321), and true-up's config offer then names no key for it.

Rationale: the question of which name yields exists only while the stack tool sets a project-named variable to the run tag. Once the `stack` key retires, `ports` stays only as a setting the port registry reads, and no other config name competes with a port name.

messages.text: Prevent import cycles, and leave where shared code lives to each project. Step 2 of the reuse rule checks that an import does not close a cycle, as well as what the import weighs. Where reuse would close a cycle, the agent breaks the cycle so every import points one way, in whatever shape the project's own organization calls for. An import placed inside a function to dodge a circular-import error is a defect, fixed by breaking the cycle. A project checks for cycles with a tool for its language.

options.label: A
options.text: Prose rules only: step 2 weighs an import's direction, shared code moves down to the lowest package both callers may import, and a function-local import placed to dodge a cycle is a defect fixed by moving the code. Cost: a written constraint with no check, against the cheatsheet's rule that every constraint has one.

options.label: B
options.text: Prose rules plus a suite lint check: the project declares its layer order in ok-planner's configuration, and a new check in the suite's lint fails an import against it. Cost: per-language import parsing in a lint that today reads comments and compose files, a new configuration key with its config check and true-up offer, and an amendment to [decision:project-chooses-its-lint-checks](.ok-planner/design/decisions/project-chooses-its-lint-checks.md).

options.label: C
options.text: Prose rules plus a project-checked layering rule, after the stack-ports precedent: the suite states the rules, and a project with more than one package declares its layer order and checks it with an import linter for its language. Cost: a project that wires no such linter gets the text alone, and the suite cannot check the wiring.

options.label: D
options.text: Leave layering to each project's subjects and practices. Cost: the reuse rule keeps sending agents across package boundaries until an owner writes a practice, and every project words the rule its own way.

problem:
Plumbline's reuse rule tells an agent to import an existing function from wherever it sits, and no Plumbline rule says where shared code lives or which way an import may point. In a project with several packages, agents who follow the rule build import cycles between packages, so no package can be maintained on its own. The cheatsheet commits the suite to "Strict DRY: semantically identical logic lives in ONE place" and to "Every written constraint needs a check that fails on violation: layering → dependency lint", but no rule tells a project to declare its layers, so no project has a layering to lint.

The mechanism: section 6 of [plumbline-coding.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/docs/plumbline-coding.md#L66-L72), "Import, never copy", says in step 1 "Where it exists, import it", and in step 2 "Where a dependency-split rule seems to block the import, read what the module actually imports before assuming." Step 1 sends the agent to the function's current home. Step 2 weighs how heavy an import is and never which way it points. Each reuse can add an edge up or across the package graph, and nothing mechanical refuses a cycle: the suite's lint runs five checks, comment hygiene, citation resolution, no tests, compose ports, and compose labels ([plumbline:LINT_CHECK_NAMES](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/plumbline#L187)), and none reads imports. Where Python refuses a circular import at load time, an agent moves the import inside a function to get past the error instead of moving the shared code down.

The owner reports the harm from the LineScout platform (package `gridiq`), which runs Ruff and declares no layers: one import cycle of 12 units spanning its main services, three two-unit cycles, 13 imports of the project's own modules placed inside functions, two of them on the big cycle to dodge circular-import errors, and 12 of the 79 root modules, which act as the shared base, importing service packages. Each import was reasonable inside its task; together they keep the owner from splitting the platform into independently maintained parts. That evidence lies outside this tree.

The owner asks for rules that cover at least: the project declares its layer order and a lint fails an import that breaks it; before importing from a sibling or higher package, the agent moves the code down to the lowest package both callers may import; an import placed inside a function to dodge a circular-import error is a defect fixed by moving the code; and step 2 weighs an import's direction, not only its weight. The canonical rule files and the lint are this project's shipped product, so the change is the project's own, and the copies under `.claude/rules/` follow on the next `/ok`. Every line added to the rules costs context in every session, since [concept:cheatsheet](.ok-planner/design/concepts/cheatsheet.md) keeps that layer small. [decision:stack-ports-checked-as-a-suite-rule](.ok-planner/design/decisions/stack-ports-checked-as-a-suite-rule.md) is the precedent for a suite rule a project checks with the suite's lint where it applies, with a project lint, or with both. No corpus artifact speaks to import direction or layering.

The ruling decides what the suite prescribes about where shared code lives and how a project checks import direction.

recommendation.text:
State the layering rules in the suite and have each project check them with its own import linter. Step 2 of the reuse rule weighs an import's direction as well as its weight. Shared code lives in the lowest package every caller may import, and an agent moves a function down before importing it from a sibling or higher package. An import placed inside a function to dodge a circular-import error is a defect, fixed by moving the code. A project with more than one package declares its layer order and checks it with an import linter for its language. Record the rule as a suite decision beside the one for stack ports.

Rationale: this follows the stack-ports precedent, where the suite states a rule that holds for every project and lets a project check it with a lint that reads its own formats, which import graphs are: every language parses imports its own way, and mature import linters already exist for the common ones. It gives the cheatsheet's "layering → dependency lint" a layering to check, which prose alone (A) does not, and it costs a few lines of rules text where a suite check (B) costs a per-language import parser, a configuration key, and an offer. Leaving it to practices (D) leaves in place the rule that sends agents across packages, which is the harm reported. The flip case: if owners commonly run multi-package projects with no import linter wired, the rule stays text there, and a suite check (B) earns its parser, starting with the languages the suite's own users ship.

ruling.text: Prevent import cycles, and leave where shared code lives to each project. Step 2 of the reuse rule checks that an import does not close a cycle, as well as what the import weighs. Where reuse would close a cycle, the agent breaks the cycle so every import points one way, in whatever shape the project's own organization calls for. An import placed inside a function to dodge a circular-import error is a defect, fixed by breaking the cycle. A project checks for cycles with a tool for its language.

title: Plumbline says to import shared code but never where it lives, so agents build import cycles

messages.text: The ruling on stack-lifecycle-delegates-to-project-tooling replaces the mandated stack tool with optional helpers. Removal of a run's docker objects moves to the new docker sweep helper, which the reference .ok-planner/bin/stack calls. Revise this issue so its question, what evidence lets the tool conclude a run made no docker object when the daemon does not answer, targets the docker sweep helper.

after.label: A
after.text: The sweep reads silence as nothing made: where the daemon does not answer, the sweep removes nothing, reports that the daemon did not answer, and exits zero. Cost: a run that made labelled objects and lost its daemon before teardown ends with nothing that records those objects, in the reference tool and in every project's own teardown alike.

after.label: B
after.text: The sweep reports silence, and its caller decides: where the daemon does not answer, the sweep removes nothing and exits with a status of its own, distinct from success and from a refused removal. The reference stack tool records every daemon answer it observes, before and after its start command, on a failed start as on a passing one, and treats that status as done only for a run that recorded no answer. Cost: every project teardown that calls the sweep handles one more exit status, and a daemon started and stopped inside the start command, or started by a later verification step, still escapes the reference tool.

after.label: C
after.text: The sweep takes the evidence as an argument: the caller tells the sweep whether the run ever reached docker, and the sweep reads silence as nothing made only where the caller says the run did not. Cost: the evidence each project's tooling must collect, such as a probe around its own start, becomes part of the helper's interface, so the sweep no longer stands alone.

after.label: D
after.text: Silence leaves a docker-pending record: the sweep reports silence as in B, and the reference stack tool releases the run's ports and deletes its folder but keeps its entry marked as owing a docker sweep, which a later cleanup runs once the daemon answers. Cost: on a machine where docker is installed and never started, a pending entry stays for every run and the registry listing grows without bound.

before.label: A
before.text: The start-time answer decides (the code now): the corpus says a run whose daemon answered neither before its start command nor at `down` made no docker object. Cost: a start command that starts and later loses the daemon leaves labelled objects with no record.

before.label: B
before.text: Any answer the tool observes decides: the stack tool also probes the daemon after the start command exits, whether the start passed or failed, and `down` skips docker only where none of its probes answered. Cost: one more docker call on every `stack up`, and a daemon started and stopped inside the start command, or started by a later verification step, still escapes.

before.label: C
before.text: The answer at `down` alone decides: `down` skips docker whenever the daemon does not answer, and deletes the entry. Cost: a run known to have made labelled objects loses its entry while the daemon is stopped, and nothing later removes those objects.

before.label: D
before.text: An unreachable daemon leaves a docker-pending entry: `down` stops the process group, deletes the folder, and releases the ports, but keeps the entry marked as owing a docker removal, which a later cleanup performs once the daemon answers. Cost: on a machine where docker is installed and never started, a pending entry stays for every run and the registry listing grows without bound.

problem.after:
The ruling on stack-lifecycle-delegates-to-project-tooling replaces the mandated stack tool with optional helpers. One of them is a docker sweep that removes every docker object carrying a run's label or whose compose project equals the run's tag, and the reference `.ok-planner/bin/stack` calls it at `down` and in its cleanup. The sweep finds those objects by asking docker's daemon. Where the daemon does not answer, the sweep cannot list them, so it cannot tell a run that made no docker object from a run whose objects stay on disk while the daemon is stopped. No corpus artifact says what the sweep reports then, or what lets its caller treat the run as taken down. [story:verification-leaves-no-artifacts-behind](.ok-planner/design/stories/verification-leaves-no-artifacts-behind.md) owes the owner a way to have each run's artifacts removed once the run is over, and [decision:run-artifacts-recorded-by-the-stack-tool](.ok-planner/design/decisions/run-artifacts-recorded-by-the-stack-tool.md) says `down` removes every container, image, volume, and network that carries the label.

The mechanism the sweep inherits: [stack:start_run](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/stack#L723) probes the daemon once with `docker version`, before it runs the start command, through [stack:docker_reached](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/stack#L581-L589), and records the answer on the run's registry entry. At `down`, [stack:removal_steps](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/stack#L638-L653) asks [stack:docker_out_of_reach](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/stack#L592-L593) whether the recorded answer was no and a fresh probe also fails; where both hold, it skips every docker removal, and `down` deletes the entry. The cleanup's [stack:in_use](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/stack#L816-L837) skips its running-container check on the same test. Where the start-time probe answered, `down` tries every docker removal, and a refused removal keeps the entry for a later cleanup, as [decision:run-artifacts-removed-with-the-run](.ok-planner/design/decisions/run-artifacts-removed-with-the-run.md) requires. The start-time answer lives on the reference tool's registry entry. A sweep usable alone, called from a project's own teardown, takes a tag and holds no such record.

The state of play: sprint certification of `2026-10-14-stack-lifecycle` (run converge-2026-10-15T011914) added the skip as defect i17. Before it, a run that made no docker object, taken down on a machine with Docker Desktop installed and stopped, kept its entry and its leased ports behind four docker refusals, and every later cleanup refused it again. The skip fixes that machine. Its gap is a run whose daemon came up after the start-time probe: a later stopped daemon reads as proof that the run made nothing. Under the helpers the question splits in two: what the sweep reports when the daemon does not answer, and which caller holds the evidence that a run never reached docker.

The ruling decides what evidence lets the docker sweep, or the caller that runs it, conclude that a run made no docker object when the daemon does not answer.
problem.before:

problem:
True-up never counts a file as a caller of a retired suite script where the file sits below any folder in the project that holds both `admin/true-up` and `admin/ADMINISTRATION.md`, so it removes the retired copy even where such a file still calls it. The mechanism: true-up finds callers of a retired script with `git grep -F` over the tracked files, repoints what it can, files an intake issue for each file it cannot repoint, and keeps the retired copy while such an issue names it. A path the running payload also carries is that proof, and it survives the working tree moving past the installed release, which the content match the fixer rejected does not. Its one false positive is a payload file newer than the installed release, which costs a kept copy and an issue until the next release: the cost the decision already accepts. messages.text:
Keep `.ok-planner/bin/stack` as the one required tool for drives and tests, and cut the friction for projects with their own stack tooling:

1. `stack down` also removes every docker object whose compose project equals the run tag. Coding rule 10 asks that each docker object a run makes be removed, by that compose project, by the run label, or by the stop command, and no longer requires the label. The lint retires its `compose-labels` check.
2. A new optional key, `stack.prepare`, names a command `stack up` runs under a lock before the start command, for setup many runs share. Its output outlives the run, `down` and `cleanup` leave it alone, and the project prunes it. A shared image or folder is named after its inputs, never `:latest`. A failed prepare opens no run.
3. `stack up` treats a port as taken when it fails to bind over UDP as well as TCP, and when a docker container on the host publishes it.
4. The stack tool serves drives and tests only. It mints no tag for release images, and a project's release scripts use a tag source of their own.

Replace the mandated stack tool with optional helpers, and return the process to v25.3.0's model, where each project runs its own stack commands.

1. The process prompts run the project's own commands. `/converge`'s drive and `/audit`'s deployments run the commands that the "Drive commands" section of `.ok-planner/review/project.md` names, as in v25.3.0. No prompt names a suite helper.
2. Remove the mandates: coding rule 10, the cheatsheet's "Per-run artifacts and verification stacks" section, the lint's `compose-ports` and `compose-labels` checks, and the `stack` key in `.ok-planner/config.json`. `ports` and `port_range` stay only as settings the port registry reads.
3. Ship helpers that a project may call from its own commands, each usable alone:
   - a tag generator at `.ok-planner/bin/run-tag`, with the same path and output as v25.3.0;
   - a port registry that leases and releases ports per tag, treats a port as taken when it fails to bind over TCP or UDP or when a docker container publishes it, and lists stale leases;
   - a docker sweep that removes every object carrying a run's label or whose compose project equals the run's tag;
   - a process-group helper that starts a command in a group of its own and later stops the group.

   `.ok-planner/bin/stack` stays as a reference start and stop built from the helpers, for a project with no stack tooling of its own.
4. Describe the helpers in a reference document outside the always-loaded rules, with the tag and port advice from v25.3.0's cheatsheet.
5. Each project's own tooling owes the stories `concurrent-stacks-without-port-collisions` and `verification-leaves-no-artifacts-behind`, and `/audit` checks them there.
6. True-up moves a v26.0.0 project's `stack` declaration back into its "Drive commands" section.

The suite fixes both the stack lifecycle and its one implementation: [decision:stack-tool-runs-each-run](.ok-planner/design/decisions/stack-tool-runs-each-run.md) makes [`.ok-planner/bin/stack`](.ok-planner/bin/stack) "the only way to mint a run tag", and [decision:ports-leased-from-a-project-range](.ok-planner/design/decisions/ports-leased-from-a-project-range.md) makes it the only source of a run's host ports, so a project that already runs isolated stacks with its own tooling must replace that tooling or conflict with it. The owner asks that the suite define the process and the verbs it requires, and let a project's configuration name the project's own implementation of each verb.

Observed in the GridIQ platform project (linescout/platform) on its `/ok` true-up from v25.3.0 to v26.0.0, which the owner then backed out:

- The project runs named stacks: `GRIDIQ_STACK=<name> bin/up` gives each stack a compose project name and a port block, which `src/gridiq/cli/instance.py` allocates and records in `.local/stacks/<name>.env`. `bin/dev`, `bin/down`, and `bin/device` read the same file. Drives use the stack `drive`, and build tasks start stacks of their own, such as `machines` and `outage`. It also runs project folders with recorded port blocks, per-stack device images, and its own cleanup verbs (`driver stop-unit-stacks`, `driver superseded-images`).
- The `port-range` offer would make `stack up` lease 17 `GRIDIQ_*_PORT` values into the start command's environment. Compose prefers the shell environment over `--env-file`, so leased ports would override the stack file's ports, while the project's readiness checks and `bin/dev-account` read the file. Two allocators would disagree about one stack's ports.
- Declaring `stack` with the project's existing commands works for `/converge`'s drive, but [coding rule 10](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/docs/plumbline-coding.md#L104-L121) sends every build task through `stack up`. A fixed `start` command then starts one shared stack for every concurrent builder, which take it down under each other. A start command that names the stack after `$RUN_TAG` avoids that, but the project then carries two lifecycles.
- Rule 10 also requires `${OK_RUN_LABEL}` on every compose service, volume, and network, and the lint's `compose-labels` check flags 57 sites across the project's three compose files. The project's own teardown removes its stacks by compose project, so the label adds nothing there.
- True-up keeps the retired `.ok-planner/bin/run-tag` while four project scripts call it, and files one intake issue per caller with no drop-in to repoint to.

The process the suite defines holds for this project: a run gets a fresh tag, isolated ports, a start, a stop, and a cleanup of stale runs. Only the implementation differs.

ruling.text:
Replace the mandated stack tool with optional helpers, and return the process to v25.3.0's model, where each project runs its own stack commands.

1. The process prompts run the project's own commands. `/converge`'s drive and `/audit`'s deployments run the commands that the "Drive commands" section of `.ok-planner/review/project.md` names, as in v25.3.0. No prompt names a suite helper.
2. Remove the mandates: coding rule 10, the cheatsheet's "Per-run artifacts and verification stacks" section, and the lint's `compose-ports` and `compose-labels` checks. `ports` and `port_range` stay only as settings the port registry reads. The `stack` key in `.ok-planner/config.json` stays only as a setting the reference stack tool reads: `.ok-planner/bin/stack up` with no command runs the key's start command, and nothing else in the suite requires the key.
3. Ship helpers that a project may call from its own commands, each usable alone:
   - a tag generator at `.ok-planner/bin/run-tag`, with the same path and output as v25.3.0;
   - a port registry that leases and releases ports per tag, treats a port as taken when it fails to bind over TCP or UDP or when a docker container publishes it, and lists stale leases;
   - a docker sweep that removes every object carrying a run's label or whose compose project equals the run's tag;
   - a process-group helper that starts a command in a group of its own and later stops the group.

   `.ok-planner/bin/stack` stays as a reference start and stop built from the helpers, for a project with no stack tooling of its own.
4. Describe the helpers in a reference document outside the always-loaded rules, with the tag and port advice from v25.3.0's cheatsheet.
5. Each project's own tooling owes the stories `concurrent-stacks-without-port-collisions` and `verification-leaves-no-artifacts-behind`, and `/audit` checks them there.
6. True-up leaves a v26.0.0 project's `stack` key in place, and writes "Drive commands" lines that call the reference stack tool: a `stack-start` line that runs `.ok-planner/bin/stack up` and a `stack-stop` line that runs `.ok-planner/bin/stack down`.

title: The stack lifecycle runs only the suite's own stack tool, so a project with its own stack tooling cannot adopt it

options.label: A
options.text: A project marks, in its review facts, that its instance stories drive one at a time; with the mark, the drives verb files each instance drive after every other driver and chains it after the one before. Cost: one new setting, parsed by the review tool and described in the seed facts file and the converge skill.

options.label: B
options.text: The drives verb always files instance drives one at a time after every other driver, with no setting. Cost: every project with instance stories loses their parallelism, even on hosts with room to spare.

options.label: C
options.text: A numeric limit in the review configuration sets how many instance drives run at once, and the drives verb chains them into that many lanes; a limit of 1 gives option A. Cost: a new configuration key with a seed default and true-up handling, more code than option A.

options.label: D
options.text: Make the drive step's concurrency cap settable per project. Cost: it slows the shared-stack drivers too, and it does not stop instance drives from overlapping each other.

options.label: E
options.text: Leave the drive order as it is. Cost: on a host that cannot fit three stacks, the instance stories are never proven.

problem:
The review tool's drives verb starts every drive that needs a throwaway instance of the product at the same time as the shared-stack drivers, and a project has no way to make those drives wait, so on a host that fits two full stacks but not three the drives time out and the story goes unproven, against [decision:drive-tries-each-story-as-a-user](.ok-planner/design/decisions/drive-tries-each-story-as-a-user.md)'s aim that each run tries every story.

In drive mode and in sprint certification, `/converge` starts one shared product stack and then runs one driver agent per story, up to 8 at once. A project lists its stories under two headings in its review facts file ([seed project.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/review/seed/project.md#L39-L45)). A story under "Stories that drive alone" changes state other drivers read, so it runs after every other driver, one at a time. A story under "Stories that drive on an instance of their own" needs a deployment the shared stack cannot give, so its driver creates a full stack of its own. [review:cmd_drives](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/review#L1108) files every story not on the alone list with no ordering ([line 1146](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/review#L1146)), instance stories included, and chains only the alone stories after the rest ([lines 1148-1151](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/review#L1148-L1151)). The instance list changes only the brief's folder, never the order. [review:story_lists](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/review#L1045) refuses a story named under both headings, so a project cannot put an instance story on the alone list to make it wait. The drain loop has one concurrency cap across every task ([drain.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_tasks/drain.md#L7)) and no limit per kind of drive. [converge SKILL.md step 3](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/SKILL.md#L78) describes this filing, and step 6 ([line 114](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/SKILL.md#L114)) chains the confirm drivers the same way.

The GridIQ project hit this on a 16-CPU host with an 8.3 GB Docker VM. Three stacks drove the load average to about 24. The instance's identity provider answered token requests in 10 to 54 seconds, so the drive's CLI sign-in timed out four times while the same drive's browser steps passed. The merge step ([SKILL.md:80](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/SKILL.md#L80)) sorts such failures as `environment`, so the run reports no false defect, but the story stays unproven on every run on that host. The behavior is unchanged at v26.0.0.

The fix lies in project-owned source: the review tool and the converge skill under `plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/` are this repo's shipped product, and only their materialized copies are suite-owned. No accept-list entry covers the harm, and the corpus says nothing about drive ordering, concurrency, or instances: [decision:stack-tool-runs-each-run](.ok-planner/design/decisions/stack-tool-runs-each-run.md) is silent on concurrent runs on one host. The ruling decides whether and how a project can make its instance-story drives run one at a time after the shared-stack drivers.

recommendation.text:
A project can mark, in its review facts, that its instance stories drive one at a time. With the mark, the drives verb files each instance-story drive after every other driver, the alone stories included, and chains each after the one before, so at most one instance stack runs beside the shared stack. The confirm drivers follow the same order. Without the mark, instance drives keep running beside the shared-stack drivers as they do now.

Rationale: the review facts file already carries the one ordering fact the drive honors, the alone list, so a mark beside the instance list keeps drive ordering in one place and in one idiom, and leaves a project with room to spare its parallelism. Option B costs every project its parallelism for a limit one host shows. Option C buys a lane count no project has asked for, at the price of a new configuration key and its true-up handling. Option D slows the drivers that cause no load and still lets instances overlap. Option E leaves stories unproven, which defeats the drive's purpose. The flip case: if a second project shows that the right limit depends on the machine rather than the project, so that one checkout needs serial drives on a laptop and parallel ones on a larger host, a numeric limit as in option C serves better; if every project that lists instance stories turns out to need them serial, option B removes a setting nobody leaves off.

title: Instance-story drives run beside every shared-stack driver, and a project cannot make them wait
